-despite the fact that he opposed us when we tried to achieve the same results when the bill was in the House of Commons.
I would refer first to the change with respect to applications for writs of habeas corpus. As the Minister of Justice is aware, this is a matter that was discussed at considerable length in our own committee on which the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis) and the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy)

Criminal Code
were our representatives a year ago. It was their contention, as it was the contention of members from other parties on the committee, that the rule respecting habeas corpus should remain the way it was. The minister succeeded in persuading the majority to go along with the change he proposed, and that change was included in Bill No. 7 when it went from this house to the other place.
By virtue of the ninth of the proposed amendments now before us, the Senate has now put the law respecting habeas corpus back in the position in which it was prior to the introduction of this bill. We think that is a good idea, and we are glad the Senate has made that change. I might also say that the proposal that the question of habeas corpus be reconsidered was the subject of a subamendment moved by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) when we reached third reading of the bill in this house. Therefore I am sure he as well as others will likewise be pleased that this change has been made.
Another change included in these amendments has to do with the reading of the riot act. The third of the ten amendments proposed by the Senate calls for the insertion of certain words after line 42 on page 24 of Bill No. 7. The proposal is that the words "if he is satisfied that a riot is in progress" shall be inserted in clause 68. The effect of that change would make clause 68 read as follows:
A justice, mayor or sheriff or the lawful deputy of a mayor or sheriff who receives notice that, at any place within his jurisdiction, twelve or more persons are unlawfully and riotously assembled together, shall go to that place and, after approaching as near as safely he may do, if he is satisfied that a riot is in progress, shall command silence and thereupon make or cause to be made in a loud voice a proclamation in the following words or to the like effect.
Then follows the formula that has to be read out on such an occasion. As I say, we are glad that that addition is being made, namely, the inserting of the words "if he is satisfied that a riot is in progress".
As we indicated when we were in committee on the bill-I recall particularly the remarks made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis)-we are still not satisfied with the law respecting the riot act in all of its details. We are concerned in particular as to the various persons down the line who can read the riot act; but at any rate this is a slight improvement, and we welcome it as such.
Most of the other changes proposed by the Senate amendments are technical in character, and we see no objection to any of them. Indeed, there are several others that we welcome.

There is another word I wish to say, Mr. Speaker. It is this: 1 am sorry that Their Honours did not pay the same attention to the amendment we moved to third reading in this house as they appear to have paid to the subamendment that was moved at that time. As I indicated a moment ago, there was a subamendment asking for reconsideration of the clauses having to do with habeas corpus. Their Honours have paid attention to that request. But there was also our amendment in this house asking that reconsideration be given to clauses 365 and 372, having to do with criminal breach of contract and with mischief. I regret that Their Honours did not see fit, as a result of their consideration, to recommend changes in those two clauses along the lines that we advocated when the bill was in the house, in order that the rights of labour might be fully protected.
I recognize, Mr. Speaker, and I am reminded of it by the look in your eye, that we cannot at this stage discuss matters beyond the scope of the amendments proposed by Their Honours, and the look in your eye is getting to the point where I realize I must not transgress any further. I merely express my regret that these sections have not been altered as we suggested, but we are pleased to welcome such improvements as Their Honours have made in this bill.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to the one amendment, or the one change, that has been made in the contempt of court proceedings. I do so because there is still an opportunity for the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) to deal in committee with a problem that is not solved merely by providing the right of appeal. This subject has been discussed earlier. The right of appeal in itself provides some measure of protection in a field where protection did not exist in the earlier provisions of the code; but I submit that there is still reason to give consideration to the introduction of something that would offer a guide to the courts in determining what shall be contempt in the face of the court or from outside the court, and also some gauge as to what the penalty should be.
Perhaps it is only when we come to discuss a subject of this kind that we find to our surprise that there are still mediaeval survivals of law that we have inherited. The British system of law that was adopted in this country from the long-established practice, and incorporated in the Criminal Code for the whole of Canada, has carried forward not only the provisions of the code itself, but certain other long-established practices. It

is necessary to go back a very long way to find the root of this extremely important question of contempt of court. One might say that before 1066 it was the law of the jungle in many respects. After that date, kings began to appoint lawyers to represent and to adjudicate the issues arising between individuals among the people and also between the crown and the people. Later it was found that grievances against the crown itself needed to be dealt with. This led to the appointment of a lawyer to consider these grievances, and that was the genesis of the chancellery division of the court in the United Kingdom which has given so much to our law. However, those judges in the early days, answerable only to the king and in no sense to parliament, were of necessity compelled to protect the authority of the courts. Since they acted in large measure simply upon their appointment by the crown and not under laws passed by parliament, it was natural that they themselves should be given authority to enforce respect for the courts over which they presided.
In those days it became necessary to devise very stern measures against those who in any way indicated a lack of respect for the authority of the courts. We have inherited that common law practice. Bit by bit some attempt has been made to define different types of contempt of court. As was pointed out on earlier occasions, there have been amendments to the Criminal Code dealing with specific forms of contempt. There is, however, that broad question of contempt of court by the press, by writers, either in the court or outside the court, which is yet undefined by statute and in respect of which we are still carrying on with the inherited common law practices which were adopted in this country and which leave to the judge the responsibility for deciding what the law is, the responsibility for deciding what the penalty will be, as well as deciding whether the person charged is guilty of the offence and subject to punishment for that offence. The right of appeal from such a decision, which will now be accorded if the proposed amendment is adopted in regard to appeal from punishment for contempt of court, will undoubtedly be a substantial improvement. It will undoubtedly offer some opportunity for a second consideration of the circumstances under which the statements were made, and the appropriate penalty which should be imposed.
Nevertheless, I would point out that this is still not consistent with our fundamental principles inherent in the rule of law that every person shall know what the law is, and that before they can be haled into court 83276-378
Criminal Code
and punished there must be some provision which defines the offence and measures the punishment that should be meted out in the event that the person is found guilty.
We still will have no such definition of the law. We still will have no such measure of the penalty. What happens in the case of an appeal is simply that we multiply the number of judges whose discretion will be exercised in determining what the law is and what the penalty should be.
In saying this I am not, nor is any other member of this house, in any way reflecting upon the judgment exercised by the judges of this country, nor is any hon. member of this house questioning the necessity for some procedure by which respect for the authority of our courts can be maintained.
It is obvious that when criminal proceedings are taking place there should be some procedure by which the judge responsible for the fair trial of the individual or individuals being tried for any offence shall be able to assure the fair, impartial, and unprejudiced trial of the individual or individuals affected. I am sure there is not a single hon. member of this house who would not feel it is essential that some such authority exist.
Having said that, can we be satisfied in the face of the evidence before us that we are observing the fundamental principles of the rule of law when we still leave undefined what contempt of court may be in the case either of the press or of individuals in commenting upon some case before the court?
May I emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that it is not only the press, but it may be an individual as well, whose comments might be challenged. I spoke of the press particularly when this subject was before us on an earlier occasion, because there have been a number of cases where contempt of court by the press has been a subject of widespread discussion throughout the country; and particularly, having regard to the fact that the offence is undefined, we are called upon to discuss this subject from a new point of view because of a warning issued by the chief justice of Newfoundland to the effect that there should be no discussion and no publication of the pleadings in civil proceedings.
I pointed out on that occasion that this is a new concept of contempt of court in this country. Ordinarily it is in fact part of the assurance of justice itself that civil proceedings may be published and that the discussion of the civil trial and of everything related to that trial may be carried in the press. This has been regarded as part of

Criminal Code
the open, public, and free trial which assures Canadians that kind of open-handed justice of which we have been so proud.
In the case of the press, which serves to protect the freedom of the individual by reporting trials of this kind, there is a very real necessity for some understanding as to what will or will not constitute contempt of court.
May I say most emphatically that I am not questioning for one moment that in the case of some of those statements published in recent years, which have led to contempt of court proceedings, which were widely discussed throughout Canada, there was some need for restraint on discussions such as then took place.
However, the recent warning issued by the chief justice of Newfoundland-with particular reference to one of the newspapers there and in fact, I believe, to both newspapers in the city of St. John's-leaves the newspapers as well as individuals uncertain as to what may or may not be discussed in regard to civil proceedings, as well as criminal proceedings, which are now before the courts in that province at this time. I am in no way referring to the merits of the issues before the courts. I am referring only to the effect of such a general warning in regard to what should be regarded as the law relating to contempt of court.
If in any one province, under our criminal law and under our inherited law, it is possible to prevent discussion of civil proceedings, then that might very well be followed in other provinces, and the long established practice of fair comment about trials in our courts might be limited to an extent where the security of the individual might conceivably be substantially lessened through the blanket of silence that could now be thrown around trials that have taken place in the past so openly in this country.
We do not want to have the right of any individual before the courts impaired in any way. We do not want the trial of any individual prejudiced. Most certainly in the case of a person charged with some serious criminal offence it is of the most vital importance that nothing shall be said by the press or by anyone else that could conceivably prejudice the jury or lessen the possibilities of a completely fair trial.
Having said that, it is equally part of our long-established judicial proceedings in this country that there shall be an open trial which shall be known to the public so that if in any individual case injustice may be done in the opinion of the public, then reform 
may be proposed to parliament itself, which is the final authority in this case. It is the parliament of Canada which must decide, and I am still earnestly suggesting that at this time the Minister of Justice consider the advisability of defining in some way what contempt of court will be, and place some guide before the judges as to the nature of the penalty that may be imposed.
I repeat that in providing an appeal we shall have provided the opportunity for a second consideration. The appellate court in each province will be able to decide whether, in the collective judgment of the judges of that court, the penalty which was declared and the penalty imposed were fair and just under the circumstances. But now that this subject is before us, in these days when the difference between the rule of law and the rule of complete state authority is perhaps the thing that defines two systems of life as much as anything else, I believe that we should take this occasion to establish the rule of law not only for the advantage of individuals in this country but for the advantage of the judges themselves who are called upon to maintain the dignity and responsibility of the courts.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would have thought that before we were asked to adopt these amendments we might perhaps have from the Minister of Justice a word as to whether the government itself concurs in every amendment proposed by the Senate to this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: In view of the point which my hon. friend has raised, Mr. Speaker, I may say that the government concurs in every amendment proposed by the Senate.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
I thank the minister for that information. Of course we are in a position where it is desirable to bring this matter to some final conclusion. The bill has now been in the process of consideration for going on, I suppose, six years altogether. We are now, one would hope, getting towards the end of this session and it would seem perhaps rather pointless to get into a conflict with the Senate over the details of amendments which, as has been suggested, are not in themselves extensive. To make any amendments to these proposed amendments would, of course, involve the possibility of long conferences and might just delay the passage of the bill at this session. I do not think that would be a desirable result. It is therefore not our intention to move any amendments at this stage, although I must say that I would otherwise have been somewhat tempted to do so.
The amendments that, in my opinion, the Senate should be asked to reconsider are

their first and second proposed amendments. But that is something that can be done at a later date, in another year, by a positive motion to amend the Criminal Code. Such a motion would not create the difficulties which otherwise might be created if one were to move these amendments now. I will therefore just indicate the thoughts we have on the matter so that they may perhaps be taken under consideration by the government.
In dealing with the first amendment which covers the subject of contempt of court so admirably summarized by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) a moment ago, may I say that I realize that the Senate has to some extent gone further than this house went when it adopted Bill No. 7. Since this problem of contempt of court is becoming a rather vexed one, and since some judges, I think it is fair to say, have of late shown a high degree of sensitivity as to what constitutes a contempt of court, I would think that we should provide an appeal not only against the punishment but against the conviction, even in the case of a conviction for contempt in the face of the court. The Senate has made this change. As Bill No. 7 went to them, it was necessary to obtain the leave of a judge of the court of appeal to appeal in any event. They have removed that necessity. As we had left it, if that leave to appeal were granted, the convicted person could appeal either the conviction or the sentence, even in the case of contempt in the face of the court. I think it would be desirable-and I think consideration should be given to it for another year-to provide an appeal from the conviction even for contempt in the face of the court. I am prepared to admit that there would not be many cases where such an appeal would be taken or where it would succeed. I suppose, generally speaking, we all know what constitutes a contempt in the face of the court. But in view of what I have called, and after some reflection consider to be, a tendency towards undue sensitivity on the part of some judges with respect to what is actually contempt of court and what is not, I make that observation or suggestion.
Then with respect to the second amendment made by Their Honours, as found at page 733 of our Votes and Proceedings for June 10, I must say-and I say this with due respect, and particularly with respect for the highly qualified lawyers who sat on this matter over there-that their proposed subsection 4 of clause 25 strikes me as being unnecessary and redundant. I am going to 83276-378i
Criminal Code
read to the committee the wording of their proposed subsection 4 which is as follows:
A peace officer who is proceeding lawfully to arrest, with or without warrant, any person for an offence for which that person may be arrested without warrant, and every one lawfully assisting the peace officer, is justified, if the person to be arrested takes flight to avoid arrest, in using as much force as is necessary to prevent the escape by flight, unless the escape can be prevented by reasonable means in a less violent manner.
I would ask anyone who is interested in the matter what this means. I would be glad of any assistance in establishing just what is meant by those last three lines:
... Is justified ... in using as much force as is necessary to prevent the escape by flight, unless the escape can be prevented by reasonable means in a less violent manner.
That provision seems to me to be a contradiction. In the first place, you state he is justified in using as much force as is necessary to prevent the flight. Therefore he is only justified in using force if it is necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: I wonder whether my hon. friend would permit me to interject something very briefly?

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: May I say that this clause which he is criticizing has been part of the Canadian criminal law for a great many years; I believe it has been so ever since 1892. It is the section which is provided in the existing code, namely section 41, for the protection of peace officers and persons assisting peace officers in preventing escape. The reason this section was, as a Senate amendment, introduced in the Senate is that the royal commission, the Department of Justice, the Senate and the House of Commons all had previously overlooked it. There is not any question at all as to the need for it. I am rather surprised that my hon. friend is criticizing it in any respect.

speechtext: The minister may be surprised but that does not lessen the validity of the criticism. Section 25 is a consolidation of sections 23 to 27, 29, 30 to 37, 39 and 41 to 45.

speechtext:
That may be so. This proposed subclause may be identical with the wording of one of the former clauses of the Criminal Code. However, the point is that in the consolidation produced and presented to us in section 25, the matter of using force and of the force that may be necessary to effect arrest has been fairly carefully worked out and worded. The three subsections of clause 25 as passed by the house seem to me to cover pretty adequately the circumstances under which the use of force may be necessary. The fact is that we have in clause 25 now an outline of the amount of force that may be used in the concluding words of subsection 1 which reads as follows:
... is, if he acts on reasonable and probable grounds, justified in doing what he is required or authorized to do and in using as much force as is necessary for that purpose.
Then, we have in addition the safeguard of subsection 3 which makes it clear that a person is not justified "in using force that is intended or is likely to cause death or grievous bodily harm unless he believes on reasonable and probable grounds that it is necessary for the purpose of preserving himself or any one under his protection from death or grievous bodily harm". Therefore it would appear that the amount of force which may be used is quite adequately set out in the present three subsections. We now have this one added, and I am not at all dismayed by the fact that it may have existed in exactly the same wording in one of the old sections of the code.
What I am suggesting, in view of the consolidation represented by the first three subsections of the new section, is that this one is not really necessary and that added as it is now it creates confusion because it is already set out that a person is justified in using force if necessary and therefore if it is not necessary to use force he is not justified in using it. Nothing could follow more clearly than that from the words of the present section 25. After all, the infliction of death or grievous bodily harm is already a crime. Therefore, even under section 25 you would only be justified in doing that which inflicted bodily harm if it were necessary to do it. I can see no reason for restating that simple and obvious proposition under

the proposed subsection 4 added by the Senate, particularly when there seems to be a contradiction contained in the last three lines where it says in effect that he is justified in using as much force as is necessary- again that limitation-unless the escape can be prevented by reasonable means in a less violent manner.
If he does not have to use force to prevent the escape then he is not justified in using force at all, and that would be the situation without the addition of the last words there, "unless the escape can be prevented by reasonable means in a less violent manner". In view of the consolidation represented by the first three subsections, I think there is an unnecessary and confusing addition involved in this subsection 4. If it is felt necessary to add anything at all, I think it would be more consistent with the wording of the first three subsections if the words used were something to this effect: "is justified only in using as much force as is necessary to prevent the escape by flight" or "is justified in using only so much force as may be necessary to prevent the escape by flight".
That, it seems to me, would reflect the meaning more clearly than what is set out here because, as I say, it seems to me that there is a contradiction. First you say that he is justified in using force if necessary. Then you say he is not justified in using force if it is not necessary. It does not seem to me to be necessary to add the second qualification. Therefore I think it is not the best draftsmanship which could have been devised for the purpose of this consolidation.
These are the only two observations I wish to make with respect to the proposed amendment. As I say, we would have moved an amendment ourselves, particularly with respect to the contempt matter, had it not been for the fact that at this stage of the session it might have involved us in a protracted discussion with the other place and therefore delayed the session, and also because we can give more consideration to the matter and can bring it forward as a substantive motion at another session if it should then still be considered necessary.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to debate this matter. I rise to say that I regret that it has been considered necessary to debate it at all because nothing seems more futile to me at this stage than to debate amendments made by the other place if the government, as I understand is the case, is willing to accept them. As the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) said before he sat down, these questions are far-reaching, and if changes are to

be made I think of necessity they must be made at the next or some future session of parliament when we will have plenty of time to debate them.
I have been closely associated with the study of the Criminal Code. Because of that I studied the amendments made by the other place very carefully and on the whole I think they have resulted in a slight improvement. I must admit that I could not see the reason why some amendments were made but then I am not learned in the mysteries of the law. However, I felt that they did not take away materially from what had been done by the house. There is nothing we can do now unless we wish to have a conference with the other place, and I do not think there is anything of sufficient importance for that. Therefore why should we not let this measure go through?

Mr. Speaker, the amendments made by the Senate to the Criminal Code which we have just discussed contain a reference to this particular matter. However, the Criminal Code does not come into effect until January and it is thought to be advisable that in the interval between now and that time the same provisions of the Criminal Code should apply. This bill has been considered in the Senate and comes here now, and its purpose is to make that possible.
The purpose of the amendment is to ensure that a racing association that has been incorporated in one province shall not be entitled to conduct race meetings with parimutuel betting on racetracks that it acquires in another province. It simply prevents a racing association which has a charter in the province of Manitoba, let us say, from transferring that charter to the province of Ontario or Quebec or some other province and conducting races with parimutuel betting with inspection by our department. The natural way for them to get a charter to conduct racing in the other province is to go to the province itself and obtain the right to conduct racing there rather than to simply

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, June 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Prud-ham for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Argue.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It might be advisable at this moment to discuss a point of order with respect to the amendment. On June 9, 1954, I raised several questions and deferred the final ruling with the hope that upon resumption of the debate on this amendment some

hon. members may wish to make representations. If that is not the case, I would submit that I have given further thought to the remarks that I made on June 9, and find after careful consideration that the amendment cannot be accepted. Standing order 54 says:
Whenever the Speaker is of opinion that a motion offered to the house is contrary to the rules and privileges of parliament, he shall apprise the house thereof immediately, before putting the question thereon, and quote the rule or authority applicable to the case.
In the "Introduction to the Procedure of the House of Commons" by Campion this position of an unparliamentary motion is further clarified, and at page 149 it will be found:
Amendments are out of order
(1) If they are irrelevant to the question to which they are moved, or would, if carried, produce a defective, meaningless, or ungrammatical form of words.
I should like to point out to hon. members that the two words here "defective" and "meaningless" are the ones which I am concerned with at the moment.
The amendment reads:
This house is of the opinion that in view of the present grave situation in the matter of international wheat trading the government should make an immediate declaration as to its policy respecting the marketing of our Canadian wheat surplus.
The amendment asked the government to make an immediate declaration as to its policy. Policy is within the realm of executive action. Even if the amendment were to carry, if it is the policy of the government not to say anything, well, what would be the position in this house? The house would have declared that it is its opinion the government should make a declaration of policy, and there would be no such declaration of policy, because there is nothing that we can do about it. It is for the government to decide in this particular field just what is their policy, and they may decide to say nothing about it at this time. Hon. members know that when questions are asked on the orders of the day a cabinet minister often replies that this is a matter of government policy which will be announced in due course, and there is nothing that any member in this house can do about that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would like to point out that since the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has made a declaration of policy, a fortiori this amendment becomes much more meaningless than it was in the first place. Therefore, for these reasons, I declare the amendment out of order, and if the 83276-379
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus amendment is out of order it follows that the amendment to the amendment of course must fall.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to challenge the ruling because the matter can be discussed. Simply because this is a ruling of record I would point out that in the opinion of many hon. members the statement which has been put forward as a policy was meaningless and therefore we do not yet understand what it means.

Mr. Speaker, though this particular amendment and subamendment which were before the house have been ruled out of order I propose to go on with the discussion on wheat which the amendment initiated.
I regret there has been the interruption in the discussion which takes continuity away from it and makes it more difficult to carry on the debate in an orderly manner, and particularly the fact that, under the rules of our house, when this particular motion was before the house it was not as a result possible to discuss the problem of wheat and grain marketing, for instance, when the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce were discussed the other day.
First of all, I should like to make a few comments on some of the statements the Minister of Trade and Commerce made in connection with wheat marketing. When this matter was up previously the minister of course was optimistic as usual, not as optimistic as he has frequently been in the past, but still reasonably optimistic. He stated he did not think we had such a great deal to worry about; everything would work out satisfactorily, and so on. It seems to me the Minister of Trade and Commerce pursues what might be called an ostrich policy in regard to this wheat question. In other words, he buries his head as far as possible and shuts his eyes and attempts to get the rest of the people in the country to shut their eyes to what is the actual situation. In other words, he just does not like to have the real gravity of this situation realized by the people in this house or throughout the country. He not only persuades himself that it is not as bad as it is, but tries to persuade the rest of the people. It is a form of self-hypnosis.
Speaking the other day, the minister made quite a point of the fact that, as he said, the figures as to our percentage of the world trade in wheat were very good. In fact he said that we are riding at the highest point in percentage in our history. A little later on he went on to say that we are not blasting our way into the wheat markets of the

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus world but that we are, however, holding what we have.	Well, what he meant
was we were holding not what we had or have had as a general thing for many years past. We are holding only a percentage of a very small amount of wheat going into general world trade. It is quite true that as far as wheat going into the world trade is concerned, and in the last few months particularly, we are holding our percentage; we are all right percentagewise but the fact is that when you have a percentage of a very small amount it does not help a man who has wheat to sell. It does not help our farmers who have a very large proportion of last year's crop still on hand, and it does not help the country as a whole. It certainly will not assist the country, and terminal elevators crammed with wheat at the present time, to get rid of that wheat. In other words, compared with other countries percentagewise our sales are still quite good, but the actual amount of sales is very small and of no great help, and in fact, they do not in my opinion, present a true picture of the situation.
The minister said there was no reason for any complaint in regard to the way wheat sales have been handled, and during the meetings of the agriculture committee, which took place a few weeks ago, quite a number of compliments were handed out on the wheat marketing that had taken place, and very few questioned what had been done. The minister attended some of these meetings but by no means all, and I would like to ask him to read the reports of these committee meetings and he will see that I for one questioned this policy at some length, and there can be no doubt that the inference to be drawn from the large number of questions asked was that quite a number of people were dissatisfied with the situation.
Of course, if the minister is directing his statement towards the handling of wheat marketing in past years, then that is a different matter altogether, and I would also point out that in the agriculture committee we were limited to a consideration of the
1952	crop. We were not able to discuss the
1953	crop. Therefore, as far as the recent developments are concerned, the committee was unable to deal with them at all. It was dealing with something which happened a year or two ago.
Now, the minister in his statement said that the initial price for wheat is $1.40 a bushel. That is quite correct, but what about the demand that there should be a floor under wheat? As far as the present crop


year is concerned there is a floor price of $1.40, but quite a number of people are beginning to wonder if that is all they are going to get for their wheat and whether there will be any further payment. But as far as next year's crop is concerned, the one which has now been planted and which will be harvested in August or September of this year, there is no floor whatsoever, and what the farmers of this country particularly want to know at the present time is what the initial price for that wheat is going to be. In other words, what will the floor price be for the coming year?
I think before this debate is over the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) should make an announcement in that regard. The announcements in this regard have always been made before this date in previous years, and in fact some considerable time before this. The announcement is due and certainly I think there should be no further delay.
Contrary to what the minister attempted to indicate in his speech, there is no floor price whatsoever for the crop which is now in the ground and which will be harvested this fall.
There is one thing the minister said with which I thoroughly agree and that is that if you expect to sell in a competitive market your prices must be competitive. I think it is complete nonsense to talk, as some people do, about maintaining an artificial price higher than the price at which other people are prepared to sell their wheat, because, if you do that, while the price may be all right you will not sell any wheat. The minister is quite correct in his statement that we have to meet competitive prices from other countries. I will come back to that particular matter later on but I would say in passing- and I want to make this quite clear-that we should not enter into any price war because I think that would be quite fatal. Certainly if a country such as the United States reduces the price of its wheat by 10 cents per bushel on world markets, as it did a short time ago, we must meet that price if we wish to sell any wheat.
There have been quite a lot of figures put on record in regard to this wheat situation, but I do not think the figures used are quite up to date and I do not believe they put the picture in its true light, and they certainly do not represent the true picture as far as the western farmers of Canada, and in fact the entire economy of Canada, are concerned. I have a few figures which I should like to add to those which already have been put on the record in regard to this matter.

First of all, the price for No. 1 northern wheat is $1.72J per bushel, and the price in August, 1953, under the international wheat agreement and as indicated in the wheat board report, was $2.01 J. For class II wheat it was $2.02J. In other words, since August of last year the price has dropped by approximately 30 cents a bushel. The wheat we had on hand at August 1 from the previous crop year and the crop then being harvested amounts in all to probably well over 800 million bushels, and the exact figure is probably nearer to 900 million bushels.
The value of the wheat at that time was based on $2.01 and $2.02 a bushel. What that means is that the value of this wheat has now dropped by at least $250 million. In other words, the farmers of western Canada, at present prices, are going to receive $250 million less than they had anticipated when they took in the crop last August. Of course, there has been a substantial drop since that time in the amount of wheat which has been sold, but nevertheless this means that the economy of Canada will be short of $250 million. That money would have been circulated among the retailers, wholesalers, and manufacturers of Canada, for when money like this is in the hands of the western wheat farmers it keeps circulating, and when it is cut off you have a situation much like that of a house of dominoes which falls over when one is moved.
The fact that there will be about $250 million less for the western farmers to spend than they imagined there would be when they took in their crop last August is going to have a very serious effect on the economy of the western farmers and, as a result of that, on the entire economy of Canada.
I would like to say something about the amount of wheat on hand. According to the dominion bureau of statistics the wheat in a commercial position as at May 26 of this year amounted to 341,564,000 bushels and the wheat on farms at March 31-the last date for which figures are available since they are only put out every three months-amounted to 382,666,000 or a total supply at May 26 of 724,230,000. That is an enormous amount of wheat.
Now, I have seen a considerable number of figures quoted in the newspapers recently to the effect that the amount of wheat on hand in Canada amounted to 600 odd million bushels. That figure keeps cropping up in the press from day to day, though where they get it and what its origin is I do not know. However, the figures I have given are those issued by the dominion bureau of statistics and I think that is the closest estimate there is. The amount on the farms is, 83276-379J
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus of course, an estimate, but I think the figure of approximately 724 million bushels of wheat is probably fairly accurate. On April 1, following on from that-that is two months before this-the total supply at that time again, according to these figures from the dominion bureau of statistics, was approximately 741 million bushels. I will leave out the thousands. What that means as to sales is this. That was on April 1, two months ago; on April 1, or the end of March, the total sales or disappearance, whatever you like, during April and May were, as I make it, only 16,700,000 bushels approximately.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I point out the obvious error that my hon. friend has made? He has taken the figures of stocks on farms as of March 31 as constant. Of course the stocks on the farms have been moving into the country elevators ever since then. Therefore he has made an error and I think he knows it. The figures he has given are erroneous.
Mr. Speaker, I am not making any error from that point of view. The figure for the stocks on farms-the last figure which the dominion bureau of statistics has-is for March 31.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.
I am taking that figure as being approximately 383 million bushels.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.

That is the last figure there is. In other words it was the same on April 1 as it is now. There has been a certain amount that has moved in. That is quite correct. The only figures we get on it are those I have mentioned. This amount on the farms is an estimate anyway. The figures that you must take and must use are the figures presented by the dominion bureau of statistics. They are the figures the minister used.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If I may interject again, Mr. Speaker, may I say that it is all right to use the figures on March 31 as being correct as of March 31, but if you use the figures of March 31 as being correct as of June 1, you are introducing a very serious error, as my hon. friend must appreciate.
I appreciate the fact that grain has gone in and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The hon. member sticks to his fallacy.

The minister must appreciate the fact that that is the only figure available and it is the figure on which all these various computations and so forth are made. I admit quite freely that some of the grain that was
5986	HOUSE OF
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus on the farms at that time has gone into the elevators, but not a great deal of it has gone in.
In connection with this matter I should like to refer to something that happened in the committee with regard to sales of wheat. I asked a considerable number of questions in regard to this matter and I had considerable difficulty in getting answers as to what the actual sales of wheat had been during recent months, or, in fact, the only months we were allowed to look at. Eventually we got it established that the total sales-domestic, export and everything else-for the six-months period from August 1, 1953, to January 31, 1954, were only 122 million bushels. In the previous year they had been 223 million bushels;	the	year	before	that,	228	millionbushels;	the	year	before	that	181	millionbushels;	the	year	before	that,	138	millionbushels.	It was not until we got	to one year,
August 1, 1948, to January 31, 1949, that we got down to approximately the same amount, namely 120,500,000 bushels. The year before that the figure was 137 million; the year before that it was 268 million. In other words, our sales had slipped and slipped extremely badly during this six-months period. In other words this thing has been coming on for a long time and the minister knew it was coming on for a long time in spite of all his optimistic utterances in the past. The sales had slipped to just a little more than half of what they had been the year before from August 1 to January 31 of last year. I asked quite a number of questions as to whether this-
This year.

Yes; this year; August 1, 1953 to January 31, 1954. I asked quite a number of questions as to whether this was not the most disturbing fact we had put before us or that we were discussing in the agriculture committee but the officials there tried to pooh-pooh it and laugh at it, in the same way as the minister has done and to say that sales did not mean anything, that you did not need to worry about sales. In my opinion sales are the most important thing. They are the thing that counts as far as the farmer is concerned. Unless the wheat is sold, he cannot get paid for it; and that is what he is interested in. But as I say, they attempted to tell me that sales were not important, that there was no need to worry about them. In actual fact sales have continued to shrink and shrink. In other words, the situation kept getting worse and worse as time went on instead of getting better, and sales during the past few months have been frightening. When I say "frightening" I mean frightening because they were so small.
fMr. Harkness.]

I should like to approach this matter from a different point of view. Perhaps the minister will attempt to refute these figures also. The exports during the period-this information is also from the dominion bureau of statistics and I believe the figures were used here before-of August 1, 1953, to April 30, 1954, which was the last period for which I could get them, were 186,200,000 bushels. But in the wheat board report we also find that the exports for the period from August 1, 1953, to January 31, 1954, were 138,300,000 bushels. In other words, our total exports for February, March and April-for three months-were 47,900,000 bushels. That is all that we exported. That is to say that the average exports for those three months were just a little less than 16 million bushels a month. The exports for the first four weeks in May-as was established by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) in the house a short time ago-were 14-6 million bushels; and he said that that was a terrifying figure. May I say that it is not nearly as terrifying as the fact that it is the same figure as that which has prevailed for the preceding three months.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Has my hon.
friend the figures for exports for the same three months a year ago, two years ago or three years ago?
I think I could produce them for the year before, if I had a few minutes to go through this wheat board report. However, they were very greatly over this figure, as the minister knows.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No; they were not.
Yes; they certainly were.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: For February, March and April?

Yes, the figures for February, March and April were very much in excess of that. I will find the figures here in a minute. Here are the exports for the crop year 1952-53. The exports for these four months were respectively-and that was after things had got bad-17 million, 16-4 million, 25 million and 46'5 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The hon. member is now getting into May. He spoke of February, March and April. The periods are not the same.

Mr. Speaker, the minister apparently was not paying attention. I started talking about the four months. I said that in these three months the exports were approximately 16 million bushels each,

and in May it was exactly the same thing. Exports in the first four weeks were 14-6 million bushels, which would mean an average for the month of about 16 million. In other words, the exports during that whole four-month period have been an average of about 16 million bushels and that is all.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The figure was a little less the year before.

It was a great deal more the year before. I just put the figures on the record. My goodness, Mr. Speaker, this situation seems very difficult for me to understand. I am reading from the report of the minister's own board and I have just read the figures as to what the exports were for May of last year as being 46-5 million bushels; then he says they were less the year before.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Not February, March and April.

When one cites figures of that sort and then hears statements made which are so contrary to the reports put out by the minister's own department it makes it very difficult to carry on a reasonable debate on the matter. Apparently the minister is just not willing to see any reason. Not only does his optimism blind him as to what the real situation is but he will not even admit the figures that his own people put out. As the hon. member for Eglinton has said to me, the minister takes an extremely selective approach to all these problems. He selects only what is pleasing to himself and what he thinks will be pleasing to the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
You did the
selecting. You picked the months.

The only reason I picked these months, as the minister knows, is that they are the last four months, and I am trying to bring the picture up to date. I am much more disturbed about the whole situation than the minister appears to be. The situation is bad and he should know it is bad. He is the one who can do something about it but unfortunately he will not even admit that the situation is bad and that our exports have fallen to this extremely small amount.
As a matter of fact, although our exports during that period only amounted to just over 60 million bushels for four months, the picture is even worse than that because, as we learned in the committee, there were forward sales as of January 31, the beginning of this period, amounting to 21 million bushels. In other words, all the sales that have been made during this period only
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus amount to some 41 million or 42 million bushels. The sales picture seems to be much worse than the export picture and our anticipation of future deliveries is getting worse all the time instead of better. That of course is one of the reasons why the sales picture is important. It is on that basis that we make our exports.
The sale of wheat is a government responsibility. The government has a monopoly in the sale of wheat through the Canadian wheat board. As it has that monopoly, with the result that the farmers cannot sell their wheat to anybody else, the government must assume the responsibility for selling this grain. They have not been selling the grain. Sales have been going down. The situation is getting worse all the time. The farmers still have large amounts on their hands which they are not able to deliver and there is another crop in the ground which will be ready to harvest in two or three months. From one point of view particularly it is a great misfortune that the government has come to be looked upon as the only source, so far as the grain business is concerned, for information, assistance of any kind or anything else along that line.
As the result of the government monopoly in the sale of wheat the people of eastern Canada do not understand the situation. I run into people all the time, even members of the House of Commons, who, whenever an interim or final payment on wheat is made, will say to me: Oh, the government is giving you fellows another handout. Because the government has this monopoly in the handling of wheat many people in this part of the country do not understand the fact that the interim and final payments which the minister announces in the house are not government money. A whole lot of people think that it is government money which is being given to the prairie farmers when it is their own money which is being paid to them on the basis of wheat sold and so forth. As I say, government control of grain has produced an unfortunate result in the minds of many people in eastern Canada. Every time an announcement is made of a payment with respect to grain they think that the government is giving a handout to the west, which is complete nonsense.
With respect to the present situation, I thought that the minister's statement that we must meet competitive prices was sound sense. We must do that. I do not think there is any question about it. In that regard there is an article in this morning's Gazette from which I should like to quote briefly. It
5988	HOUSE OF
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus is by Sydney Gampell and is datelined "London, June 14". The article reads in part as follows:
After, as before the 10 cent price cut, and at either the minimum or the maximum price of the international wheat agreement, the wheat market is still artificial. In what amounts to a busted corner, there is no real market and no real price.
Unfortunately I think that is all too true, and under these circumstances, as I indicated earlier, it seems to me that there is no value in the idea a lot of people in the east particularly have, people with whom I have had private conversations, that if we cut the price another 10 or 20 cents a bushel we will sell a lot more wheat. I do not think we would sell any more and we might not sell as much. To cut prices and enter into a serious price war would be the very worst thing that could happen to the economy of this country and the wheat market generally. 1 am glad to see that an observer in London corroborates that view. The article continues:
If the oversupply and the overproduction in the exporting countries were thrown on the market for what it would fetch, it might be lucky to fetch so much as a dollar a bushel. Some of it might go begging as a gift. If the United States could find places inside or outside the iron curtain to make gifts of wheat with any political advantage or even without positive political disadvantage, it would probably be glad to give the surplus wheat away. It has already made some not insignificant attempts.
How the exporting countries got into this mess is irrelevant. The important question is what do they do now. What they almost certainly will not do is to slash the price in a free-for-all competition for any regular commercial markets. If they allow a sharply falling market they will sell less wheat, not more.
I would hope that attention will be paid to what was pointed out previously by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) among others, and that the government will maintain the closest possible consultation with the other big holder of wheat available for export, the United States, and will put forth every possible effort to ensure that there is nothing in the nature of a price war, in other words, that another drop on their part or another drop on our part does not take place. It seems to me that the only hope in the present circumstances, until a different cycle of weather rights the situation, is to try to maintain the price as close to the present level as it can be maintained, and that can only be done by co-operation and consultation with the United States. It would seem to me that must be the government's chief effort at the present time not only so far as the western wheat farmer is concerned but also from the point of view of protecting the whole economy of the country.


From all I have heard, it does not seem to me that the government has met its responsibility in that regard in recent months. I think one great lesson that we have learned, or that I hope we have learned, from the present situation is that the wheat agreements which were sold to us particularly by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) as the cure for all the uncertainty of agriculture in western Canada have not succeeded in doing that. They have proved to be a complete disappointment. I think the history of the years since the war has demonstrated the fact that there is no security for agriculture in international or intergovernmental wheat agreements because the importing countries enter into these agreements when it is advantageous for them to do so, and when the price is falling and it is not advantageous they do not enter into them or if they have they do not fulfil the agreement as was the case with one or two nations which signed the international wheat agreement.
Wheat has had an unfortunate history in the post-war period. The western farmers lost several hundred million dollars through having to sell their wheat at less than the market price and now they have no security so far as wheat delivery, price, quantity or anything else is concerned. I would hope that as the result of this experience we have at least learned one lesson, that these things do not provide security and there is no use counting on them to do so.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as I said, the government is responsible and has been responsible all the way through for the selling of Canadian wheat. They have not met that responsibility. We have all this wheat on hand that has not been sold. We find the farmers in an increasingly difficult situation, and particularly is that going to be the case if this next crop proves bountiful. Therefore I would move as an amendment to the motion, seconded by the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Charlton):
That all the words after "That" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that the government has failed to deal effectively with the problem of marketing Canada's wheat surplus."

I rise, Mr. Speaker, to take part in this very important debate. The announcement by the government on June 7 of the lowering of the price of the three top grades of wheat by 10J cents a bushel was a blow below the belt to the western farmers. The ramifications of that policy, which I maintain is the forerunner of a fire sale policy, cannot be overemphasized. We have already heard

one or two members in this house representing the western part of Canada, who have indicated their concern.
I can agree in only one respect with the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Hark-ness), who has just spoken. He stated that the responsibility rests with the government. There can be no denial of that statement. I cannot, however, go along with him when he indicates that he is more or less in agreement with the government's policy.
I do not believe I could have indicated the reverse more strongly.

Then, the hon. member will have to explain it, because after all he did not lay down any policy. He took it upon himself to more or less explain the wheat stock situation, and then he did say, I believe he will agree, that the price of wheat must be competitive.
In this group we have in the past supported the idea of the international wheat agreement and orderly marketing of grain. We have supported the principle which has been followed by the Canadian wheat board, and the principle of marketing wheat under that board. Here, I believe we have a diversion from that program that has been pursued in the past. In spite of the fact that we in this group have, during this session, asked the government to indicate its wheat policy and also to give some indication of what the farmer should do in respect to seeding of the crop this year, we have not to date received any information from them as to what the government's policy is to be in the future.
Indeed the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has castigated members of this group who tried to get some statement from him as to the initial price for wheat this year. Then, after the western crop has been seeded again, here we have the government announcing a policy on June 7 which, as I say, can only make the devils laugh and the angels weep. Surely we could have a policy in this country by which our agricultural producers could have stability and security. I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), both of whom I am happy to see are in their seats, that if they allow the decline in prosperity in western Canada, it is going to affect every last home in Canada. We in this group are not coming here to suggest blue ruin in the west. We recognize that Saskatchewan, our own province, is in a prosperous state.
Many of the farmers are in the happy position of having paid off some of their pre-war debts; they are in the happy position
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus of having grain in their bins; they are in the happy position of having been able to purchase farm machinery, even at the high prices, in order to farm more efficiently. But I do want to say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture that we are not going to sit in this house and wait until the agricultural situation deteriorates to the point of depression. I am happy to see that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Mang) is in his seat. He represents a riding that is just north of mine. I do not believe he performed any useful service to western agriculture or to himself when he took it upon himself the other night to indicate that there was not a very serious situation in western Canada.
You are right there.

Later on in my remarks I shall deal with what he said. It is sufficient at this time to say that there are, however, people who appreciate the situation. If anyone in the house thinks the farm members from western Canada are asking for something unreasonable, let him look at the full-page advertisements that the great firm, the T. Eaton Company, have published lately in the Toronto Globe and Mail. Province by province, these advertisements have indicated the economic situation.
On June 12 last the full-page advertisement concerned Saskatchewan. We are mighty proud of the success we have had in Saskatchewan, and of our ten-year record with a C.C.F. government. All those resources were there prior to 1944, Mr. Speaker, and we feel very fortunate that the resources we have in that province are being developed for the people by the C.C.F. government. The C.C.F. government did not put the resources there; that was the work of Divine Providence. We are happy to note that we have 40 per cent of the oil reserves in Saskatchewan alone. This advertisement illustrates that in Saskatchewan 70 per cent of the population is rural and 60 per cent of the provincial revenue is derived from the land. One can readily see from that that we are dependent upon the returns we get from agriculture.
At one o'clock the house took recess.
The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, at one o'clock I had been discussing the serious situation which has arisen owing to the announcement on June 7 when the government indicated that the price of wheat

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus for the three top grades would be dropped by 10J- cents per bushel. The failure of the government to announce early in the year the policy it might have in regard to wheat has left agriculture seriously concerned as to what the future holds. While the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has indicated to the house-and has been reported in the press to the same effect-that he does not foresee any price war in the sale of wheat, it does not in any way quiet our fears that the government is now launching upon a program which may spell disaster for agriculture in Canada.
Not only have there been various press comments in this connection, but I should like to quote a press report appearing in the Ottawa Journal of Saturday, June 12, which states:
Jake Schulz, president of the Manitoba farmers union, Friday protested trade minister C. D. Howe's statement that Canada will cut the price of wheat again if necessary to protect this country's share of the world market.
Mr. Schulz said in a statement the minister's comment will "be a shock to many western farmers".
Mr. Schulz, as president of the Manitoba farmers union, represents a large organization of farmers in that province. In addition to that, a press dispatch appearing in the Manitoba Co-operator of June 10 indicates that the federation of agriculture has sent a telegram to the minister requesting that the government should not engage in any fire sale of Canadian wheat. I would quote from the press report as follows-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. Hon members should not quote opinions of associations or newspapers published outside the house reflecting or commenting upon proceedings in the house. When the hon. member was making his first quotation I was about to rise. Now that he has embarked upon a second one I think it is my duty to remind him that citation 265 in Beauchesne's third edition states this:
It is not in order to read articles in newspapers, letters or communications emanating from persons outside the house and referring to, or commenting on, or denying anything said by a member or expressing any opinion reflecting on proceedings within the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No.

I am
happy the minister shakes his head, because all along we have been asking the minister to indicate the policy of the Canadian government. If we are to have a policy of orderly marketing and exporting of wheat, it cannot be one whereby, as soon as we have stocks of wheat on hand, we are going to throw it on the open market, regardless of price. I know very well that time and again the Minister of Trade and Commerce has repeated his statement that it would be useless to cut the price of wheat to increase sales because the demand is not there.
So I do not think the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) added clarity to the situation when he spoke in Regina. His speech is reported in the Ottawa Journal of June 14. The Minister of Agriculture said that the piling up of wheat in the finest storage facilities in the world is playing right into the hands of the market. I do not know what the Minister of Agriculture meant by that statement. If he means that by having some stocks of grain on hand we must embark on a fire sale policy, then it is like hunting for a jet-black cat in a dark room where there is no cat. It is just as clear that you cannot get any solution from that sort of thing. What we in the C.C.F. advocate is the principle of the ever-normal granary. In view of that, the Canadian stocks of wheat should be recognized as a safeguard for short crop years.
After all, Mr. Speaker, we are fighting an ideological war throughout the world. We are trying to indicate to those countries of the world that the kind of society in which we live is the best society for man. We are fighting to win over men's minds to our way of life. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) rises in his place and asks: Where are those hungry people? I have only to refer him to the publication put out by the government entitled: "Current Review of Agricultural Conditions in Canada." I do not intend to read it. Perhaps I would not be permitted to read it to the house. This is a government publication which gives a favourable impression of the foodstuffs existing throughout the world. It goes on to
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus indicate the hunger and the need for the uplifting of nutritional standards in various parts of the world.
I submit to the house that if we are fighting a war to win men's minds and to do away with hunger, then of course we have to play our part, and play it in a full way, in order to see that these countries that are undernourished and underfed and hungry are sufficiently fed. Not so many years ago Sir John Boyd Orr, then president of the food and agriculture organization, indicated that about two-thirds of the people went to bed hungry every night. If that is the condition that exists, surely in Canada we are not going to have a policy which is not going to allow our agricultural producers who have cooperated with the government to produce sufficiently huge stocks of wheat for a world which needs food.
At page 5749 of Hansard the minister seemed to indicate that in interviewing the members of the agricultural conference meeting here in Ottawa he was led to believe that farmers from western Canada were not in a bad financial position. He indicated that, according to his interview with those representatives, only about one per cent of the farmers needed financial assistance in the way of loans. I want to point out to the house that it may be quite true that a lot of the western farmers are still in a financially liquid position. But on the other hand, there are straws in the wind that indicate that the situation existing in western Canada is not as rosy as the minister suggested.
According to the dominion bureau of statistics figures, in 1946 the prairie indebtedness stood at $367 million. In 1952 it had increased to $486 million. Then again the loans from chartered banks increased from $283 million in 1952 to $318 million in 1953. Under the farm improvement loan plan, in 1951 the farmers of the prairies borrowed $85 million; in 1953 they borrowed $98 million, an increase of 33 per cent in the number of applications.
Let me take the agricultural picture over the country. In 1951 the figure stood at $2,811 million. In 1953 it had dropped to $2,674 million, or a decrease of $137 million. The situation is serious; and, as I indicated before lunch, we from western Canada are not concerned entirely with the prairie provinces. We recognize that if the agricultural situation is affected adversely it will in fact bring the whole economy down to that level. That is exactly what happened in the 1930's when agriculture was not receiving its fair share of the national income and prices were at a deplorable level. People
5992	HOUSE OF
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus were out of jobs and our whole economy suffered. Already we have had delegations coming to Ottawa from the agricultural implement industry and the textile industries indicating an increase in unemployment in Canada. Indeed, it has reached an all-time high. Therefore we are asking the government to hold the price line and to use its policies and its power to sell our wheat at prices which will guarantee the producer a decent standard of living.
In Saskatchewan we have made tremendous gains in the last ten years. We do not come here from that province asking for a handout. The thing we are asking for here is nothing short of a just, fair and equitable policy for western agriculture. At one time our province of Saskatchewan was called nothing but a hard luck province. In the last ten years we have been successful in raising the standard of living. We have been successful all along the economic line in order to give our people more security.
I hold in my hand a booklet published by the government of Saskatchewan, showing ten years of progress under that government. I commend it to all hon. members, because it shows in an unmistakable way the progress made in that province. We are not content, sir, to sit idly by and to see our people go back to the conditions that existed prior to 1944. I remember full well that during the election-and I believe it was the type of advertising used by Liberal candidates all over the country-Liberal candidates said: "Vote Liberal and keep Canada prosperous." I think the people supported the government and returned them to office on that basis. As the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said the other day, we should try to keep the record straight. He emphasized that point of view in his speech many times. I say now, let us keep the record straight. This government told the people of western Canada that if they voted Liberal they would have continued prosperity. Well, in the years from 1951 to 1953 agriculture has been put in an adverse position, when you compare the returns to agriculture with the cost of production. According to the dominion bureau of statistics figures there has been a decrease of about 16 per cent. That could very well end up in a tailspin, where our people once again would be losing their farms and where the general picture for agriculture would be disastrous.
What I am saying to the government today is that we in this group support the principle of orderly marketing. The government should assume the responsibility of taking over surplus stocks of wheat in Canada.
When you look over the submissions made to the cabinet by the Canadian Federation


of Agriculture over the years you will see that they have advocated to the government that surplus stocks of wheat in Canada should be stored and that the agricultural producers should not suffer from having those surplus stocks. It would be good policy, Mr. Speaker, for the government to undertake a policy of storing a thousand million bushels of wheat in Canada as a reserve either for war or for scarcity.
I do not agree with the Minister of Agriculture that having surplus wheat in this country should mean disaster, because that is the only interpretation I can take from his remarks as published in the Ottawa Journal of June 14. If the government undertook that policy, it would not mean of course a lot of money being spent on storage, but it would mean that the agricultural producer would have money in his pocket to buy the farm machinery. The farm machinery workers would be able to return to work, and so would many people who are today unemployed. Of course, anything may happen; but the Minister of Trade and Commerce has indicated on many occasions over the past three years that the crops we have had were likely to continue. What better type of husbandlike direction could we have from the federal government than the government taking over these stocks and storing them until people require them throughout the world?
I am sure he will agree with me when I say that the time will come when we can market these stocks of grain at a very decent price, a price which will meet with the support of the farmers, and one which will not cost the Canadian people one single red cent.
Today we have enough money to meet essential commitments in our defence program. There can be no question about that. And if we need more money for planes or guns the government can find it. This year we are spending about $2 billion for defence purposes. That may well be necessary, but I would point out that today we are not necessarily fighting a war involving guns and planes. We have to make people believe in the free way of life we have in the western world, and if that means anything at all it means security to the people of Canada, and livelihood, job and home security to the farmers throughout the length and breadth of the land.
We are not going to be able to put across any of the principles we cling to in regard to a better way of life to the peoples of the Far East and Asia unless we can have such a program here. It must be rather difficult for the people in the underprivileged countries to accept these views when they hear that in

Canada, although we have produced more cars, machinery, and more of everything else, we are starting into another economic tailspin.
I would therefore urge the Minister of Trade and Commerce to tell the farmers today, even though it is rather late in the day, what the initial price for wheat this fall is going to be. The government should buy, store, and pay the farmers for wheat, which could be stored against future commitments. For in my opinion the only way in which we are going to get the importing countries to adhere to any agreement is to assure them that they can obtain their requirements of wheat at an agreed price and on the date when it will be required in future.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hope my hon. friend is not going to put words in my mouth. I did not say it was "probable" and I did not intimate what he implied. That is what concerns farmers at the present time. I noticed in the Ottawa Journal the other day that the president of the farmers union of Alberta, Mr. Henry Young, has urged the government to announce that they will not allow the price of wheat to fall below the support price under the international wheat agreement. speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I make a comment? I cannot think of a more bearish statement any government could make at this time.
