Wheat-Marketing of Surplus we have is an initial payment. Let me point out to the minister that there is a fundamental difference in principle between an initial payment and a floor price. An initial payment is usually set sufficiently low so as to ensure that the average price received during the year will be higher than the initial payment. On the other hand a floor price or a support price is usually set sufficiently high so as to ensure that the price of agricultural products will not be allowed to fall sufficiently low to reach an uneconomical level.
As an example, let us take the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act. Under that act provision is made whereby the government can guarantee an initial price up to 80 per cent of the average price of the past three years but, as a matter of practice, the government has usually guaranteed that initial payment up to only 60 per cent in order to be certain that they will not suffer a loss. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) himself pointed out that there is a big difference between that act and the Agricultural Prices Support Act, because under the Agricultural Prices Support Act provision is made not for an initial payment but for a support price and that support price is tied to the price of other commodities, under section 9. I therefore say that the farmers would feel a great deal happier today if they knew that a support price was going to be maintained under wheat.
The minister has also stated in the past that he does not think the Canadian consumer should be taxed in order to subsidize the price of wheat. On the other hand, I never heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) object when the Canadian farmer was taxed in order that the people of Canada might receive wheat at a lower price. When the price of wheat to the producers was kept below the world market price, actually what was happening was that the producer was being taxed in order that the consumer could receive wheat at a lower price. There is no difference between the two. In the one case you are taxing the people to subsidize the price of wheat at a fair level. In the other case you are taxing the farmer in order to keep the price of wheat down to what the government considered to be a fair level at that time.
If the government, as a matter of policy, fails to stabilize the price of wheat at a level that returns to the farmer a fair price they will, in my opinion, be committing a definite breach of faith with the farmer. In 1941-42 when the price ceiling was put on, the prime minister of the day, in a broadcast, announced to the farmers that he appreciated the fact that they were expanding


their production in spite of the fact that a price ceiling had been put on; and he guaranteed that in compensation the prices after the war would be stabilized at a fair level. That was a definite promise made by the prime minister of this country in 1943.
In 1945 the then minister of trade and commerce announced a post-war policy on the marketing of wheat. He said that policy would be not to try to obtain the full world market price for wheat sold to our allies but that it was the intention to sell wheat for less than the world market price because he considered that we had a moral obligation not to charge our allies the maximum price we could get, having in mind the great contribution they had made in that war. When I replied to the speech made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I pointed out that we were prepared to support that policy, that we realized that we in Canada had a moral obligation to help our allies by not charging them the maximum price but that we must recognize that it was a moral obligation of the people of Canada as a whole and not merely that of the farmers. I pointed out that any losses suffered as the result of that policy should therefore be borne by the Canadian people as a whole and not by the farmers alone; in other words, to whatever extent losses were suffered, the farmers should be compensated for that loss.
We all know what happened. I am not going to place a lot of figures on the record- they have been placed on the record so many times already-to show what those losses were. We all know that there was a substantial loss as the result of selling wheat under the British wheat agreement and selling wheat to the consumer in Canada at the same price instead of obtaining the price for class II wheat, which loss has been estimated anywhere from $300 million to $500 million. All the farmers received against that loss so far was a payment of $65 million.
As I say the prime minister referred to the fact that the farmers had made a sacrifice and that they could rest assured that they would be compensated for it by a stabilizing program after the war. The Minister of Agriculture also referred to the same thing in the past. If the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce represents government policy in this country, and if they are opposed to the people of this country being taxed in order to subsidize agricultural prices in order to maintain them at a fair level, then it can mean only one thing. It means that the price to the farmer is to be governed by the so-called law of supply and demand. If that is to be the policy, then the

farmers of this country would be justified in reducing their production in order to try to keep the price higher.
Would the Minister of Trade and Commerce agree that the farmers would be justified today in reducing their production in order to keep prices higher? If prices are to be made subject to the law of supply and demand, that is the only protection the farmers have unless the government is prepared to step in and to place a support price under farm products. I should be interested in knowing whether that was government policy.
I think a declaration of that kind should be made. I think it is only fair to the farmers that they should be told by the government whether their policy is this:	We want you
to reduce production; we are not going to guarantee a higher price but you can look after the situation yourself by doing as other industries do, namely reduce production, and that reduced production will force prices up. Personally, we in this group do not favour such a policy because if we had two or three years of drought we would have a situation in the world where there would be widespread famine.
In his speech the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that it was a fallacy to suggest there were starving people or starving nations in the world today. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce reads what is put out by the food and agriculture organization, I think he would be impressed by the fact that consistently over the past five years they have been stressing the fact that unless the nations that have the ability to expand the production of food do so, there will be widespread starvation in the world. In their recent publications they have referred to that point on a number of occasions. When the food and agriculture organization met in conference in Rome last fall one of the first statements issued there-and I quote from the Western Producer-was as follows:
The United Nations group said in Rome, Italy, on the eve ol a three-week conference that opened November 23, that its latest surveys showed a trend back "to the dilemma of the '30s with excess food co-existing with hunger."

The report notes that "if, because of the fear of surpluses (in the more developed countries), present production plans were scaled down, the result might be a continuation of past shortages and inadequate levels of nutrition, for there can be little doubt that a high rate of population growth will continue at least for some years to come. I.F.A.P. recommended that production of such crops as cotton, grain and potatoes be reduced and that production be increased for such commodities as animal proteins not in surplus supply at present.
If the government feels it would be advisable to cut down the production of wheat and increase the production of other commodities it could encourage action of that kind by a policy similar to that carried out in the United States where the farmers were given the option of maintaining their production of wheat at the present level and taking a cut of around 40 or 50 per cent in the price of wheat or cutting their production of wheat by 25 per cent and continuing to receive the support price of $2.21 a bushel, that is 90 per cent of parity. A policy of that kind no doubt would bring a substantial reduction in the production of wheat and would bring about an increase in the production of other farm commodities that may be needed at the present time. In prescribing prices under paragraphs (a) and (c) of subsection (1), the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.
I have been reading, Mr. Speaker, from the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
This applies to all agricultural products, with the exception of wheat. However, it was stated when the act was enacted that wheat would be dealt with on the same principle, but that it was not necessary to include it in this act because it was under the control of the wheat board.
This, as I see it, is sound, just and fair -that agriculture should be assured of supported prices in difficult times, that it will get fair returns as compared with those engaged in other occupations. That policy, I think, is sound; it is the law of the country today, and it is a policy that I am satisfied the Liberal government, who put the law on the statute books, will carry out.

And I want to say this to hon. members opposite that, speaking for the great agricultural constituency of Rosthern, which I have the honour to represent in this House of Commons, I am satisfied that that will be satisfactory to the fair-minded people not only of Rosthern but of the whole of Saskatchewan. This attempt on the part of the C.C.F. to play to the gallery has been seen through pretty well by all of Canada, and I think it is going to be seen through in Saskatchewan, and that the handwriting is already on the wall for the C.C.F. in that province.
You didn't do much writing.

What is basically wrong, what is basically unjust, and what is basically unfair to your fellowman will not ultimately succeed. I have that much faith in my fellow Canadians, and in my fellow citizens from Saskatchewan.
Now, in regard to the amendment of the Progressive Conservatives, it reads:
This house regrets that the government has failed to deal effectively with the problem of marketing Canada's wheat surplus.
That amendment, Mr. Speaker, is really an attack not only upon the government, which has appointed the wheat board and which carries on this work through the wheat board as its instrument, but it is an attack upon the wheat board itself, because if there has been a failure to deal effectively with the marketing of our wheat, then of course the people who have failed to do that are the wheat board. It may be said that it is the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I do not think that anyone suggests for a moment that he is engaged in the marketing of wheat. True he is consulted in regard to the matter, but the one who takes the responsibility for doing the marketing of wheat is the wheat board. There have been attacks upon the wheat board in the past. I have deplored them because I think our wheat board system has saved our producers in western Canada literally hundreds of millions of dollars over the last ten years. I regret this continual attack, on every possible pretext, upon the wheat board and the wheat board system of marketing grain.
That is the sort of thing that everybody from western Canada, of all parties, if they think that the wheat board is a good thing, should deplore. I have a great deal of respect for the gentleman who moved this amendment and I am sorry that, coming from western Canada as he does, he saw fit to move this particular amendment. I am sure that

in doing this he was not speaking on behalf of the vast majority of farmers in western Canada.
The farmers in western Canada are apprehensive, Mr. Speaker, over these constant attacks upon the wheat board and our present system of handling grain. One of the proofs of that is to be found in an advertisement which I have in front of me. It is in a paper dated April 10, 1954, just two months ago. It was inserted by the Saskatchewan wheat pool. I submit, to you, Mr. Speaker, that they would not pay money to put such an advertisement in the paper if they were not apprehensive about the constant attacks being made upon our present grain handling system. Here is what this advertisement says: It is headed: "Some grain facts." The subheading reads: "Canadian exports, wheat and flour." It continues:
This year, August 1 to January 31, 138,700,000 bushels. Ten-year average, August 1, to January 31 from 1943 to 1953, 137,700,000 bushels.
During that period the ten-year average was 1 million bushels less than we exported last year during the same period. The wheat pool wants to draw this to public attention. They put in black letters that the record during the present year is better than the average by 1 million bushels. I continue: The next subheading reads:
Deliveries to elevators western Canada, all grains: This year, August 1 to February 28, 400 million bushels; ten-year average, August 1 to February 28, 1943 to 1953, 373 million bushels.
The farm deliveries during the seven-month period of this crop year covered by this advertisement are better than the ten-year average, as pointed out in this advertisement, by 27 million bushels. The advertisement goes on to say:
Orderly marketing keeps grain moving. These are the facts. Don't be misled. Saskatchewan wheat pool, head office, Regina.
There is the attitude of the farmers of western Canada. They believe that we have a good grain handling system and they are apprehensive about attacks on it. They believe that the rest of Canada will be led to believe that we in the west are not satisfied with it; that it has failed; and that there will be the feeling that it should be changed. They want everybody to know that they the farmers in western Canada are satisfied with the present system of handling our grain, and the people who are real friends of that system will not seize upon a time of difficulty to attack it, Mr. Speaker, as is being done here today. Surely the time when the wheat board and the present system of handling grain needs support is now, when there are great difficulties.

Don't burst a blood vessel, over nothing.

They do not need support when things are going well. The time when that system needs support is when there are difficulties such as there are at present, and the real friends of the present system of marketing can be found when people seize the first chance to attack it, Mr. Speaker. The people of western Canada are observing what is happening today in regard to this problem.
You are just setting up a straw man and knocking him down.

This is as complete and wholehearted an endorsation as you would get of any human institution, and yet this house is by this amendment asked to deplore, to condemn indirectly, something that our farmers in western Canada have fought to get for the last twenty years, at least, and are glad to have; and they are not going to abandon it because we have entered into a period of some difficulty.
This view is shared by members of all parties when they are speaking more or less as they should speak on behalf of the farmers. Well, I find at page 32 of the proceeding of the committee on agriculture a definite question is asked of a member of the wheat board. Mr. Riddel in answer said:
Yes, I think our markets in the Orient have been expanding during the past number of years, particularly in Japan, the Philippines and Hong Kong.
We heard the members of the board going over the work that they were doing in pressing the sale of our grain in all the countries of the world. Anybody who heard the evidence must have been impressed with the splendid case they made out and with the

That is a definite, bald assertion by a member of the wheat board and yet when the Minister of Trade and Commerce rises in his place in the house and points out that we are holding on to our markets, that we are keeping our share of the markets, he is attacked because he defended the work being done by the wheat board. One of the things with which everyone agrees is that we should not have a fire sale if we are to retain a fair price and hold our share of the markets of the world, because other people will want to do the same. If we try to get more than our share of a dwindling market in any way, shape or form, then the others are going to try to defend their position, and I think all hon. members agree that would be undesirable. We can put a floor price under wheat but that is not going to get rid of our grain. The floor price might get you a few votes, but what I am dealing with is the problem which confronts us in western Canada of getting rid of our grain.
At an adequate price.

A high floor price is not going to get rid of the grain. It is suggested, for example, that we accept sterling in payment for our grain. Yet, we are told that Great Britain has had enough of having her currency taken in payment for various things she could not pay for during the war. She built up a debt with Egypt and India of about $12 billion and when she tried to repay that debt during the period following the war she was faced with millions of dollars of so-called unrequited exports.

My hon. friend says "So what?" That meant that when Great Britain came out of the war, struggling valiantly to regain her position, she had to meet that demand in exports for which she was getting nothing in return. She had this millstone hanging around her neck and as she struggled to the position where she could stand on her own feet and again become one of the leading nations again in regard to trade, commerce, banking, and monetary matters, she had to cope with this colossal handicap. The leaders of British opinion have taken the attitude that they want no more of this business of buying things for which they cannot pay and giving sterling which they know they will have to repay ultimately, for they believe in keeping their word.
It is therefore suggested here that we take sterling in payment and then expect Britain to pay it back later. But the British say, "No, thank you".

Their attitude is that they do not want that sort of thing. During those remarks he agreed with the Minister of Trade and Commerce that if the minister gave him certain information at that time, he would sit down. He did not do that.
He sat down, and then he got up again.
The hon. member went back on his half of the agreement. The hon. member for Assiniboia is spokesman for that group in agricultural matters.
Mr. Speaker-
Sit down.

Just let me finish this thing The house had a demonstration of just how good their word is, and what an agreement means to this kind of people. We have had plenty of experience along that line in Saskatchewan.
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order-
Sit down.
-the hon. member is trying to prove, by what he has just said-
There is proof right on these pages, and everybody saw it.

The hon. member for Assiniboia will defend himself, but I insist that the hon. member for Meadow Lake withdraw

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As I said before, although I followed the discussion with some care I did not get the impression that the hon. member for Meadow Lake had made any imputation. Nevertheless if the hon. member for Meadow Lake imputed that the word of hon. members opposite him could not be believed, he will, of course, withdraw. I am sure he would be glad to withdraw.

If that were the case, I would do so, but I am talking of a particular case in this house and every member saw it. There is nothing to withdraw because I take it that if the hon. member sitting there, and who has risen so many times on questions of privilege and points of order, had not agreed with the exhibition put on at that time he would have gotten up and taken exception to it. It was at that time he should have risen on points of order and questions of privilege, when the member for Assiniboia put on that exhibition. If the hon. member did not agree, that was the time to say so.
What I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, is that that is the situation with socialists generally, that is the trouble we have internationally, because you cannot make agreements with these people. They do not keep their half of the agreement. Possibly if we got rid of that type of thinking in the world we would not be faced with this debate now.
You could not trust Mr. Attlee?
To give these gentlemen credit, this type of thinking was not originated by them. It was first invoked in Grecian times when Philip of Greece used this kind of-
Let us get back to wheat.

We are into this subject now, and we might as well go through with it. When Philip of Greece wanted to take over a neighbouring country, he immediately said he was good friends with them. They knew then they were going to have their throat cut next morning. This system of attack has been taken over by the socialists and is still used. When the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics want to take over some country, they immediately sign a friendship pact with those people. They move in and cut their throats next morning, then take their goods and chattels.


Well, it was along this line that Demosthenes made his first Philippic or his first speech against Philip of Greece.
Let us get back to wheat.
I should like to just quote a remark made by Demosthenes on this type of thinking. It is a remark from the first speech by Demosthenes against Philip.
Mr. Speaker, when do we get to wheat, which is the main point in this discussion?

I think the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) will enjoy this, and very likely it will help him in the future to sell hardware. The quotation is as follows:
And who is it that deceives the state? Surely, it is the man who speaks not what he thinks.
Is that what you are doing?

The quotation continues:
What greater crime can an orator be charged with than that his opinions and his language are not the same.
I charge you.

How often do we find the opinions of these gentlemen and their language not the same? They get up and make speeches inside this house, then you talk to them outside of it and find they have different opinions altogether.
When we get back to the subject of wheat we find that we have had a lot of discussion about wheat and the plight of the farmers in the west. When we first came to Ottawa for this session last fall we had a new crop of C.C.F.'ers fresh from the hustings in Saskatchewan, who had been expounding a theory out there. They had been saying: if you send us down there we will be a voice for you in the parliament of Canada. What a voice they have been! If we read the speeches in Hansard of last fall referring to agricultural matters, what do we find? The hon. members opposite preached blue ruin to such an extent that the leader of that party got up the other day and said that was not the situation they wanted to convey. The hon. member for Moose Mountain did a little more work along that line today.
Anyone who is engaged in trade, either personal, national or international, knows that if you want to sell something you advertise it. The type of business you get in return depends upon the kind of advertising you put out. Of course if you advertise that you have so much Wheat you do not know what you 'are going to do with it, the farmers are

broke and have to sell and do not know what they are going to do with this wheat, as has been done by some gentlemen here who are the voice of the farmers in the west, naturally you are going to get results from that advertising. I believe that one of the reasons we are having this debate, and having all the trouble in selling this wheat, is that kind of advertising from those members here.
Why do you not tell that to the Minister of Trade and Commerce?

If these members had genuinely wanted to help the western farmers, they would not have put out that kind of advertising.
The system of advertising in ancient days was for peddlers to shout their wares. When one went to London then one did not find these street peddlers selling their wares by saying they were poor quality, or they had such a stock that they despaired of selling it. Everybody knows that a fish peddler does not sell his fish by shouting, "rotten fish!" He will say that the supply is very limited, and that the fish are the very best.
But these gentlemen opposite come down here and shout "rotten fish!" They have done that for several days on several occasions, and now the pigeons have come home to roost. And they are surprised. Well, it is indicated that they think there is some soft-pedalling should be done, with respect to this blue ruin talk, by the remarks the other day by the leader of the C.C.F. party, and those of the hon. member for Moose Mountain.
I was interested in some of the other theories offered by the hon. member for Assiniboia the other night. He said that the government south of the line has a much more progressive policy in handling grain than we have. Of course he was speaking about their subsidy policy. My hon. friend from Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) touched upon that. Then, the hon. member for Assiniboia said that this federal government, the one we have here and the one I have the honour to be a member of-
Since when?

-has never done anything about floor prices. Well, I suggest to the house that no other government in this country, except this government, ever did anything about floor prices. And if the farmers in the west are up against the decision of either taking the word of this government that it will stand behind them, or taking the word as set out in the amendment moved by members of the opposition- especially after the demonstration that was 83276-380i
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus given to them as to what their word is worth, and in this very debate, by the hon. member for Assiniboia-well, I think there is not much doubt about where the farmers will stand, and in whom they will have faith.
Certainly we are up against a difficult situation in view of the surpluses in the United States. That very policy that they have in the United States is the cause of our trouble, and I do not think anyone will disagree with that. When that policy was put into effect it was an incentive proposition to persuade the farmers to grow grain, because the supply was short and our allies had to be supplied. At that time it was considered to be a short-term policy. But having caught the tiger by the tail, the administration over there have not been too prone to let it go, because they are getting scratched a little bit while hanging on. And they will get clawed and bitten besides if they let go of it.
I think they have grown over a billion bushels of grain in that country for several years in a row. They have three quarters of a billion on hand now, and they are going to grow another billion this year. Yet they are going to provide an incentive policy down there to have them grow more. Well, I suggest to hon. members opposite, or to anyone else, that if that policy had not been followed across the line we would not be engaged in this debate. This top-heavy surplus was caused by the incentive-and under the conditions when the policy was originated, the incentive was required because the grain was required. But once that grain is available, and they have satisfied their requirements, there is not much use keeping on with that incentive.
Certainly the government over there owes its farmers a living, just as this one does. But I think when it comes down to brass tacks this government will stand behind the western farmer so far as seeing that he gets a fair return for his produce is concerned.
Does not the hon. member realize that under the present program in the United States the farmer in that country will not lose by that policy?

The farmer will not lose by it, no-that is, immediately. But how long will it be before he will lose? The farmer in this country is the one I am interested in, and he is losing by the continuation of that policy over there.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Our subamendment seeks to rectify that.

I do not want hon. members to get away with the idea that I would not

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus agree to some form of subsidy for our farmers. I would tell them definitely that that is not my idea, and that is not the idea of this government, either. When floors are required they will be forthcoming from this government, but not under the conditions we have now, not with the surpluses of grain they have in the United States where they have put on an incentive. That will not cure the situation.

Do you
believe in parity prices for farmers?

That is the trouble with the situation; the parity price they have over there is unrealistic in the light of the world market. That price might be all right if the world market were at a higher level, but not at the present time. What you want to get rid of is the incentive idea with surpluses of that kind on your hands.
You are sure getting rid of it.
It may not be the kind of thing my hon. friends would go into, because they want to have votes. That is all they are interested in. They are not interested in discussing or facing the facts.
Nonsense.

They want votes.
Another one of the dissertations of the hon. member was the proposition that we should tax and spend, tax and spend, and should go in for deficit financing. Well, I wonder if the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre goes in for that in his business? I do not think so.
He does not look like it.
On a point of order. The hon. member for Assiniboia was quoting Mr. Roosevelt.

Mr. Truman, with which he thoroughly agreed, yes. He said he thoroughly agreed with it; and that is just the point. I am glad the hon. member raised the point of order. In other words the hon. member for Assiniboia wants deficit financing in times of prosperity. What are you going to have when times are bad?
A Liberal government.

It is quite natural to hear that remark from a socialist, that we should have a policy of tax and spend, tax and spend, and that we should go in for deficit financing. Because the whole basis of the socialist theory is to get something from somebody else for nothing-you do not care whether it is from your children or your grandchildren. But so long as it is deficit

financing you are not going to pay for it. Your children may pay it after a while; and if they don't, then it will be your grandchildren or your great-grandchildren. Somebody else will be paying it, and you do not have to. That is socialist thinking. I can see where that comes in. And I was not surprised to hear that from the hon. member.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Your government has failed to reduce the national debt.
This government, since it has been in office, has reduced the national debt right along.
Oh, oh.
That's a bright one.
With the exception of the war years.
Oh yes!

And that is a horse of a different colour, of course. And nobody else has done any better in any other country. We used to hear a good deal about Australia from our socialist friends, but now we hear more about Great Britain. Well, in Great Britain, when they had their Labour government, they did not do any better nor as well at debt reduction. I hear my hon. friends laugh; they think that is funny.
The fact of the matter is that this government has made some approach toward reducing our debt, and no government that made the stand it did during the war, paid as much as it went along as this one did-and we were engaged in the same war. No other government that was engaged in that war has as good a record as this one has, in the matter of its financing, not even the United States government across the border. And certainly our record since the war is a lot better than the record south of the border. They have been engaged in deficit financing, and I do not think it has got them anywhere, certainly no farther ahead than we have got.
And so, Mr. Speaker, I think those were the main points I wished to make.
What were they, Jack?

I am glad the hon. member asked that. He wants to know what they were. One of the main points I wish to make is the reliability and integrity that people can expect from members of that group-and I still except the hon. member who has interrupted; but when he makes interruptions he must expect the answers he receives. That is the main point I wanted to make. That kind of thinking from socialists in all parts of the world is the thing that anybody will agree is causing our troubles internationally and bringing about our dilemma and our not

being able to settle differences, because you have nobody on which you can rely to settle them with.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What a tremendous contribution this has been!
Thank you, sir; it may not have been as lengthy as some of your own.
The hon. member is for lower prices for wheat.

I hear a voice from the wilderness talking about lower prices for wheat. I do not think that I would be advocating lower prices for wheat. I am not defending holding it in the bag, and certainly when it comes to the farmer deciding whether our present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) will handle our wheat to good advantage, or whether he can rely on the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), with his blue ruin talks, to get him a better price he will certainly give the nod by a slight margin to the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

Mr. Speaker, before we grant supply in this house it is a member's right to draw the attention of the government to the difficulties and problems of people in his part of the country. We are availing ourselves of that right at this time by moving that before we go into supply the government, because of the condition of world markets today, should deal with the problem of placing a floor under the price of farmers' wheat.
It is rather to be regretted that government members take this opportunity to drag in a lot of provincial politics. The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) is singing his usual song of remorse over his own failure-
On a question of privilege-
He went out like a knight in shining armour some years ago to conquer the province of Saskatchewan, and probably that is the cause of his remorse now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand that the hon. member for Rosthern is rising on a question of privilege.

Yes. I sat down at least a half a dozen times for hon. members opposite. I would point out that I rose on a question of privilege to ask a question. Apparently the hon. member does not even want to let me correct him. He suggested that I dragged in provincial politics. I said nothing whatsoever about provincial politics. I challenge the hon. member to point to one thing I said.
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus He said I wailed over my failure in Saskatchewan. I challenge him to show one thing I said in regard to that matter.

I was referring to your
wailing voice, sorrow, regret and remorse hurled across the house, and the same goes for the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Harrison).
Pretty weak.

Such knowledge and such insight, such an understanding of the people of Saskatchewan came from him. It was rather surprising that he did not do better while he was out there. He tried to build up a case for himself, and when he shouts his loudest you always know he has the weakest case. When he tries to say that the members of this party, the C.C.F., are in any way attacking or not supporting the Canadian wheat board, then he knows in his own heart that what he is trying to say is not right.
On a question of privilege.
Not only have we supported the wheat board, we have-
On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

The hon. member has no right to say that I said something I did not believe. I believe that when they say what they have about the failure to market our wheat properly, they are attacking the wheat board. I believe it.
This party has always supported the wheat board.

Hon. members opposite are very anxious to have the hon. member for Meadow Lake withdraw something that is not as bad by far as what was just said by the hon. member. He said that I said something that in my own heart I did not believe. I ask that he be asked to withdraw that in an unqualified way.

Mr. Speaker, what I said was this. When the hon. member tries to say that this party not only did not support the wheat board but attacked it, it is wrong. He knows we have never attacked the wheat board. We have always-

That is not what the hon. member said. He cannot twist and squirm out of it. He said that I said something that in my own heart I did not believe. I ask that he be directed to withdraw that, Mr. Speaker.

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member made the remark which the hon. member for Rosthern has said he did, of course he must withdraw it.
The remark which I used, Mr. Speaker, was-
Withdraw like a man.
He knows the record of the C.C.F. party has always been in support of the wheat board. We support it; we always have supported it and we never attacked it.
Withdraw.
He tried to imply we did. We did not.

The hon. gentleman is twisting and squirming. I am not surprised in view of the past attitude, but I do ask that you make him withdraw that statement. I suffered enough smears from people opposite and I am not going to stand for it in this house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Smear away.
The record stands.
I ask the hon. member to withdraw.
The record stands exactly as I said it.
I had enough smears from the people opposite. Again I say I do not accept it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member implied that the hon. member for Rosthern said something which he did not believe, then the hon. member for Yorkton realizes that he must withdraw, and I ask him to do so immediately.
Of course I would, Mr. Speaker. The record stands and what I said can easily be read in the record. It will be seen that our record stands just as clear as what I have said.
Withdraw and don't repeat it.

Another statement which the hon. member for Rosthern did not quote quite correctly was the statement that the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave to us with regard to the position of Canada's wheat. Here are the actual words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce as recorded on page 5746 of Hansard:
If you expect to sell in a competitive world, the price must be competitive with prices offered by other countries.

He said nothing there about protecting others. He goes on:
That, I think, is the situation today.
That is taken directly from the record. That statement of the situation causes apprehension among the grain growers in the prairie provinces. There is the statement without reservation that prices can go to the very bottom, and still there is nothing in the way of floor prices to protect those grain growers.
Since this house opened last November we have been telling the minister and the cabinet that a very serious economic situation was developing in the west.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: And the minister of finance in Saskatchewan has been telling the world the opposite.
Does the minister mean to say that there is no serious economic problem in the west?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am just giving the two stories, yours and that of the minister of finance in Saskatchewan.
Then there is no serious economic situation developing?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I will let you choose.

I say that a serious economic situation is developing, and it has been developing for some time. It is the same across the whole of Canada. It is not true of Saskatchewan alone. It is true of Manitoba and Alberta and the figures already prove it. The next few months will prove it even worse.
More blue ruin.
You have been predicting that for ten years.
Tune your violin.

You were out there for five of them; you know all about that. Under a Liberal set-up today the western grain growers, as compared with last year, have not only been curtailed in their deliveries, they have delivered 170 million bushels of grain less than last year. The reason for the apprehension in the west is that in the face of a drop in prices the farmer sees no possibility of reducing his cost of production along with that, and he is being caught short. We are merely asking that the government do something to protect those farmers from going into a complete collapse, and to stop prices from hitting the bottom.
Ever since last November we have been told that the situation was all right; that we

will do as well as we did last year; that we are above the 20-year average or the 10-year average. That situation has developed until the point is reached where the people here, who are trying to say that everything is all right, really believe it themselves. The minister's attitude can best be likened to that of a chap who sees someone falling out of a 30-storey window and when he had just passed the 20th storey window the watcher says: "What is he hollering about? He is all right so far."
That is a baby story.

We are asking the minister and the government to place a floor under the price of wheat so as to prevent western agriculture from hitting the bottom with the resulting collapse not only of the economy in the west but of the entire economy of Canada.
The wheat producers have done their job. We believe the Canadian wheat board has done its job. It is the policies within the government which make it impossible for the wheat board to carry out the task of maintaining prices. The producers must depend upon the policies of the federal Department of Trade and Commerce, and they have to try to maintain markets in other countries and sell their goods at a proper price regardless of the fact that Canada is a high priced economy. I know that that is difficult in view of the high prices of goods produced in Canada today. It is not this 10-cent drop in the price of wheat which bothers us, it is the situation behind that and what it implies.
The producers are entitled to some form of security and this amendment asks for that. If a price war starts the producers will be facing a very serious situation indeed. They are perturbed about how far the price is going to be cut. The minister says, "Well, we live in a competitive world and we have to meet that competitive price." But our neighbour to the south does not require the producers there to face that danger. The farmers there are guaranteed a pretty high floor under a government subsidy. We think the Canadian producer is entitled to something. We do not ask for $2.21 a bushel, but we do ask for enough to be paid so that the producer will be kept in business and so that he can continue his operations. That is the reason for our amendment.
The minister is well aware that there is a very critical situation with regard to delivery and ready cash in the west. That problem does not face the farmer in the U.S.A. The prairie farmer today is facing not only a situation of abundant crops, and lower prices, he is also facing the fact that within 90 days he may be harvesting another
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus crop. If there is no floor price and no assurance today that in another 90 days when he begins to harvest his crop it will pay him to do so, then he is obviously in a serious predicament. Can there not be some floor price under these commodities? The purpose of this amendment is quite clear. We want a floor price so that the farmer can have some assurance that it will be worth his while to continue his production and so that he can plan his production in regard to that price.
The situation in the west is severe. There is not only the matter of production, but there is also the matter of distribution and the matter of storing the crop he has already sown. The farmers in the west deserve to have a guarantee of some form of security.
The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce said something which caused some concern among hon. members here, namely, as to what could be done with regard to the disposition of the wheat. He said, as reported at page 5749 of Hansard:
Now, there is another fallacy, namely, that there are millions of starving people in this world who would be glad to get the wheat if someone gave it to them. I wish people who make that statement would just tell me where those people are and how we can get the wheat to them.
Later, he added:
I wish my hon. friend and other hon. members of this house who keep referring to the fact that there are starving peoples who would be glad to take large quantities of surplus wheat if we were willing to give it away would just remember these facts.
I do not know the minister's source of information but, according to the food and agriculture organization, a branch of the United Nations, which has at its disposal some of the finest experts in the world who have made a study of this problem, there are more than a billion people in the world today who require food and do not have enough. Surely the minister is aware that there is need for food in the world today and that that food should be delivered to those who need it.
In western Canada during the past eight years we have enjoyed a period of general expansion and prosperity. The farmer's income has been high and we recognize that. But along with his expanding income the cost of production has been expanding at an even greater rate. The cost of everything which goes into production has increased in price until today the farmers' margin is much less than it was a few years ago.
The tragedy of the situation today is not so much the drop in price but the fact that if a serious drop in price occurs today the farmers' losses can be terrific because of the terrifically high cost of production. That is

Private Bills
the reason for the very urgent demand on the part of the grain growers that a floor price be placed under the farmers' commodities so that they can be guaranteed something and the loss will not wipe them out.
If there is no floor price under these commodities then the farmers of western Canada will be placed in the same position as that of many of the fishermen in the maritimes when there was no market for their fish. They will be in the same position as the Cape Breton coal miners who now find the coal mines closing down and oil being substituted. They will find themselves in exactly the same position as the workers in the farm implement plants who are now laid off, and in exactly the same position as the automobile workers who are facing a substantial reduction in plant staff, which has increased Canada's unemployed ranks to a very critical point. The farmer has no unemployment insurance.
The Canadian producer requires some basic security and if he can get it he will continue his purchases with regard to farm machinery and the plants will continue to operate. They ask this government to consider a floor price and to maintain that price on the basis of the price maintained by the wheat board as of June 4. If that is done it will restore some faith to the producer of wheat, and guarantee some security to the entire Canadian economy. More important it will bolster up the purchasing power of all Canadians and greatly improve the situation. If that is not done then in this peacetime competitive world about which the minister speaks, thousands of producers will be wiped out in western Canada and that will reduce the western economy to niggardly existence, lower the standard of living will result, and the purchasing power of the entire nation will be affected. The economic effect of this will cause distress and trouble in every part of Canada.
The choice rests with the cabinet. On behalf of those people in the west who are undertaking the production of food and to save them from what can be economic disaster I would ask the government to make this choice immediately and assist those who face this very serious and critical situation.

The house in committee on Bill No. 472, to incorporate Canadian Slovak League-Mr. Reinke-Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.
On clause 1-Incorporation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I wonder whether the sponsor of the bill would not like to have this opportunity of saying a few words about it? He did not have that opportunity on second reading.

Mr. Chairman, in order to bring hon. members up to date and to give an explanation of what this bill is about possibly I might briefly explain the background of the Canadian Slovak League. It was founded in Winnipeg in 1932 and received its letters patent from the Secretary of State of Canada in April, 1934 and acquired the usual corporate powers that an organization of that type would acquire. The Canadian Slovak League was set up as a social and a cultural organization. I could possibly read some of the aims as outlined in the letters patent but I shall not unless hon. members would like me to do so. There are some 57 adult branches spread across Canada from one coast to the other. In all there are probably in the neighbourhood of 3,800 adults and possibly 700 junior members of the society.
This bill corresponds with similar bills which the House of Commons has already passed. The head office will be at Fort William, Ontario. It is to be a fraternal benefit society so incorporated as to have the power to create an insurance fund and a department for the aid of its members and dependents and to undertake with its members a contract or contracts of life, disability and sickness insurance as well as to provide for the investment of the funds of the said society and to define the rights of members of such society, all of which is to be for the benefit and protection of its members.

It is because it proposes to exercise these special powers that it is necessary to come to parliament and to ask for the corporate rights under this bill. The proposals which the bill contains as to membership, management, directors and bylaws have satisfied the superintendent of insurance but until the actual bylaws are approved the superintendent, of course, will not allow the society to engage in business. I understand the superintendent of insurance also has approved the provisions of the bill with reference to the maintenance of a general fund, and such matters as premiums, assessments, disposition of surplus assets and so on. I am further informed that the superintendent of insurance has been supplied with an actuarial report on the financial position of the society and that the report is satisfactory.

Clause agreed to.
