Mr. Chairman, I am sorry that I was not at the banking and commerce committee meeting at which, I understand, this bill was considered. Paragraph (c) of subsection 2 of clause 4 reads as follows:
(c) A juvenile insurance fund for providing death or endowment benefits in respect of any child, or any child under the guardianship, of any member.
I have noticed within the last several years that the regular life insurance companies are not particularly happy about writing death insurance policies for young children. I am just a little bit worried whether it is wise to have this authority granted to any benevolent society. Some recognition is being granted by most insurance companies to the proposition that some measure of death benefit, even for a child, may serve a useful purpose because even for a child there are unexpected last expenses such as funeral expenses and so on. However, I think the practice now is that insurance companies have a maximum which they have voluntarily set for themselves and that they will not accept death payment policies on behalf of minors over and beyond a certain limit. Here no limit is set or stipulated. I hope that the management of the society will bear that tendency in mind and that they will, in their regulations, definitely follow the practice that is now being followed by the life insurance companies.

I might inform the hon. member that when this bill was discussed in the committee in the presence of the superintendent of insurance the particular matter referred to by the hon. member came up for discussion. The superintendent was quite 83276-381
Private Bills
satisfied that under the provisions of the bylaws this matter would be taken care of and that it would be administered in the same manner as it is administered by insurance companies. As the matter is handled by insurance companies, I believe the maximum for a child of one year or under is $100 and that it ranges from there on up to the age of ten years, at which time they are able to procure $1,000. As I said, I believe the superintendent was quite satisfied that this provision would be handled in the same manner.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 5-Members.

I must apologize first of all, Mr. Chairman, for not having been at the meeting of the banking and commerce committee which discussed this bill. Had I been there I would have raised the point that I am now going to raise with regard to section 5. In this section I notice that there is a definition of the persons who are eligible to join this particular association. Surely it must be unique in Canadian legislation that we should provide for the formation of a body, the members of which are to be loyal to the Christian and democratic traditions of another nation. I do not quite know what that means. For instance, I do not know what are the Christian and democratic traditions of the Slovak nation, and I doubt whether many members of this committee know what they are. Most of the members are, I imagine, in the position that I am in. We know of the Czechoslovakian nation which disappeared, first of all, under the impact of nazism and which was later reconstituted to disappear later under the impact of communism. We know of a previous development in the Slovakian part of Czechoslovakia under a rather notorious individual known as Tizo, if I remember rightly, heading a pro-fascist organization.
What I am afraid of is that, in the first place, this parliament of Canada is giving official recognition to a divided loyalty on the part of residents in Canada. In the second place, we may be doing something else. I have an uneasy suspicion that here we have provision being made for what, shall I say, is the other side of the coin of totalitarian communism and that we are providing a battleground within Canada for an ideological and a nationalistic struggle between two groups of people who should, in all common sense and in all decency, be far more concerned with becoming effective members of the Canadian community.

Private Bills
It has been said of course, and said quite rightly, that our philosophy in Canada in regard to the absorption of other peoples has been that of unity in diversity, that we have attempted to provide every opportunity for the various ethnic groups who make up our population to maintain their own cultural characteristics and to make their contribution to the Canadian community on the basis of their cultural diversity. But I think that the implication might be taken from this that it goes beyond that, that we are giving our blessing to a sort of conditional loyalty to the Canadian community and the Canadian idea.
I realize of course that it is much easier for a member of the English or French speaking groups in Canada to adopt the attitude I am now adopting. I realize that for those who belong to ethnic minorities there must be a very great temptation to constitute a little enclave of their own language and ethnical group in Canada, but I do not think the parliament of Canada should condone that sort of development in our community. In fact I think it is not too much to say that we have in the past condoned far too much of that in Canada and that many of our social troubles within the Dominion of Canada have resulted from far too lackadaisical an outlook on this question of people coming to Canada and not fully absorbing the Canadian point of view and the Canadian approach.
I would specifically register my very strong objection to this Canadian parliament endorsing words in a piece of Canadian legislation by which we are to recognize that persons who are residents at least, if not citizens of Canada, are to have the right to be loyal to the traditions of another nation which is specifically set out in the legislation. Certainly the only purposes in this legislation that we can condone are quite well fulfilled in the first words of that particular section, "only persons deemed by the society to be loyal to the free institutions of Canada". That will, I think, quite effectively rule out those people who they may fear might try to join their organization, people who might be prepared to act as the agents of communist organizations abroad. I think if they insist that they be loyal to the free institutions of Canada that is all that this parliament should be prepared to assist them to do. It is no business of this parliament to promote loyalty to any other institutions, to any other democratic traditions, to any other nationalistic traditions. Our duty is confined to ensuring loyalty to Canadian traditions and to Canadian institutions.

Section 5 reads as follows:
Only persons deemed by the society to be loyal to the free institutions of Canada and to the Christian and democratic traditions of the Slovak nation-
Actually the purpose of this wording is to give the association the right to choose its membership. There have been various approaches to the same type of authority to choose membership. In some cases the marginal notes, while they mean the same, are actually different. For instance, I have a bill before me where the marginal note is "powers of association". Another one is "qualification for membership". Another uses the word "members" and another "control of society". It is my understanding that in several of these bills the language generally has been to this effect, and I am now reading from a bill to incorporate the Sons of Scotland Benevolent Association as passed by the Senate in March, 1937. The section there reads in this way:
Only persons deemed by the association to be of Scottish origin . . . shall be admitted as members of the association . . .
That is an excerpt from a bill passed by the Senate in 1937 and it refers to persons "only of Scottish origin".

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is pretty broad.
That is a different matter. That is the matter of origin.

Actually the clause in the
present bill has reference to origin as well as Christian and democratic traditions and loyalty to Canada. That is the full meaning of that clause. I might point out to hon. members that I have some other examples here. For instance, I have here an act to incorporate the St. Nicholas Mutual Benefit Association. Under "control of society" it is stated that only persons considered by the society to be of Ukrainian origin and who are of the Greek Catholic faith in communion with the Holy See of Rome shall be admitted as members of the society.

That is quite
different.

I cannot agree with my hon. friend on that score. I suppose no fault can be found with the reference in the bill before us to persons deemed to be loyal to the Christian and democratic traditions and, as I have pointed out, the reference to the Slovak nation merely refers to the fact that only those persons who are deemed to be of Slovak origin will be admitted.

I would submit that is what it should say. My fears have

not been allayed by what the hon. member has said just now, and I am very much afraid that the yardstick that is going to be used by this society is not the yardstick of devotion to the democratic ideals of Canada, which is the only thing this house should be concerned with, but the yardstick of the devotion of these people to some organization or group in Europe holding we do not know what concepts of democracy, holding perhaps some rather dubious concepts from our point of view. I suggest there is no justification for putting that in here at all and that the only purpose of it can be to separate, from the point of view of this society, the sheep from the goats. The only way in which we as the parliament of Canada can justify the separation of the sheep from the goats in this way is by deciding that it should be confined to people who are loyal to the free institutions of Canada, and I think we should confine ourselves to that. I should like to see the sponsor of the bill agree to the deletion of the reference to the traditions of the Slovak nation.

Mr. Chairman, the sponsor of the bill quoted from a bill passed by the Senate some years ago incorporating a Scottish society, but what he quoted is altogether different from what is contained in this bill. He referred also to another bill, but what he quoted from both bills in support of what is in this bill has no relation to what is in this bill at all. I do not believe there would be any objection to having this read something like this: "Only persons deemed by the society to be loyal to the free institutions of Canada and of Slovak origin." That is what is in the other bill. It refers to people of Scottish origin. It does not say they have to be loyal to Scotland before they can become a member of that society.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Does one have to eat haggis?

That is a test on which my friend would be rejected right away, but it is not provided for in the bill. I think the hon. member would be well advised to make it read "of Slovak origin" and leave all the rest out.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not often that I disagree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway but I think I should on this occasion, and with everything that has been said about the words in this clause. I have had a good deal to do with ethnic groups in the past four and a half years, and as members of the committee know there are ethnic groups and ethnic groups. Some of them are in the hands of the communists. Thank goodness, practically all of them are 83276-381i
Private Bills
not. If there is one thing in common that they have, it is that they are grateful to this country for the right of living here. They want to have a democracy here such as we have here and they are inclined to hope that the best traditions of their homeland can be transplanted here by their own actions.
Indeed they incline to the belief, perhaps we may say without too much foundation, that conditions in their homeland for their relatives are as democratic as they are here. If they cannot believe that, they at least hope that some day that will be so. When an ethnic group such as the Slovak league wishes to incorporate in its letters patent the best in their homeland, the Christian and democratic principles, whatever they may have been according to our standards, I would urge hon. members to agree to let them have that hope and to maintain those aspirations rather than to discard what to them may be valuable and may be a link with the homeland. Those words to the Slovak union mean those things that were best at home and as comparable as possible to our own. I find no offence whatever in those words.
I do not admit, as the hon. member for Nanaimo seems to believe, that there is a divided loyalty here.
There are, in fact, two loyalties but they are not divided. The loyalty, as I understand it, in the opening words is a loyalty to the free institutions of Canada. In other words, a person who belongs to this organization must begin by having that loyalty, and must also have a loyalty to the best that was in the Slovak nation, according to the interpretation that can be placed upon it by the directors of this organization, I presume. Now, that is not excluding anything in Canada. It is taking the best in Canada and trying to add to it the best of their traditions and free institutions. I hope hon. members will look upon it in that light rather than in the other way that has been mentioned.

I believe the matters raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo are interesting but not unique. There is no question of dual loyalty or partial loyalty. It is quite decidedly an undivided loyalty. I think we have to read section 4 (1) (b) of the bill which says:
The society may,
(b) promote, on the basis of Christian and democratic principles, good citizenship and loyalty to the free institutions of Canada, by educating and instructing the members of the society in the history, constitution and government of Canada;
Surely, there can be no question about dual loyalty under section 4 (1) (b). There was an act to incorporate the Ukrainian Fraternal Society in Canada, which was assented to on

Private Bills
July 24, 1943 and is chapter 39 of 7 George VI. It was a similar sort of society, and section 5 reads:
Only persons deemed by the society to be of Ukrainian origin . . . shall be admitted as members of the society:
There was a proviso in that bill which makes an impact upon this bill. One of the powers was set out in section 4 as follows:
(c) To cultivate among the members of the society fond recollections of the Ukraine, and to promote their instruction and education in its history, literature, music, arts, traditions, customs and amusements:
These people may very well have used the word "traditions" as the term was used in the act I have just quoted. Surely when people consider the words "Christian" and "democracy" as synonymous terms, and use them in that sense, this House of Commons will understand their feeling and will meet their request to carry out their intention.

Hon. members will notice under clause 2 of the bill the headquarters of the Canadian Slovak League is in Fort William; that means something. I know the Canadian Slovak League in Fort William, and they are conspicuous for their outstanding help to any members of their organization who are out of work, sick or in distress. In my opinion, they practise the Christian program, and because the headquarters of the organization is in Fort William Canada should know there is no more loyal spot in Canada than Fort William. Any society that is not loyal will have a hot time.

I would point out to the hon. member for Spadina what I am sure he does not need pointed out to him, that his argument was not a very cogent argument. It is quite absurd to quote a provision for selection on the basis of ethnic origin and compare it with selection on the basis of political opinions, which is what this clause calls for-

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, no.

It certainly does. When you speak of democratic institutions, you are making a selection on a political basis, which is entirely different from the question of origin. I would have no objection at all if this section called for the selection on the basis, not only of ethnic origin but on the basis of red-headed Slovaks or cross-eyed Slovaks or any other type of Slovak, because that would be purely a matter for the decision of this society. But when you make a selection on a political basis, and that is what this is, they are only going to select people who have a particular political

point of view. There is only one political point of view that we can condone here and that is that of Canadian institutions-
Free institutions.

No, not free institutions as they are described in other parts of the world. If you look at the constitution of the Soviet union, you will find it full of references to freedom. In fact every one of these totalitarian nations make great boasts of their free societies, their free peoples' democracies. There is only one definition of freedom and free institutions that we as the parliament of Canada can accept and that is the free Canadian institution.
I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that if this were put in there in any other way except inadvertently, then it is important we should look into it very seriously. I really believe it was put in inadvertently, and they should admit it. I do not like to see the Canadian parliament condoning in express terms a loyalty to other definitions of freedom than that comprised in the Canadian outlook, and that is what this does. I do not know, and neither does the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, what is the concept of freedom of Slovaks in Europe? What is their concept of free institutions?
It does not say Europe; it says the free institutions of Canada.
It does not.
Well, read it.

It says:
Only persons deemed by the society to be loyal to the free institutions of Canada and to the Christian and democratic traditions of the Slovak nation,-
I suggest that the hon. member and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration have no idea at all, nor can they tell this House of Commons, what are the democratic traditions of the Slovak nation. They cannot define them for us, because they do not know them.
Can you define "Christian"?

No, but I have_ a good idea of the traditions of a Canadian with regard to freedom, and that is all I am concerned with as a member of the Canadian parliament. I challenge the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to tell us what are the free traditions of the Slovak nation What are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I gather that my hon. friend from Nanaimo is trying to read into this bill a good deal that is not there. For example, he spoke first of a political decision here as to membership. Surely if he thinks about it for a moment he will realize that

this organization cannot be accused of using democracy as a word in the same sense as they do in the Soviet constitution.
How do you know?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I can assure you that the league is not of that kind, and that if it were it would not be sponsored here.

We are not
speaking about the league, we are speaking about the Slovak nation.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I will come to that. You have here a group of people seeking to be incorporated, and they are using words in their Canadian sense. They are not using words in their Russian sense, at least so far as "democracy" is concerned. If these words have any political connotation at all-and I do not agree that they have-they would be the best means of refusing membership to a communist that I can think of. And unless the hon. member for Nanaimo were to put an express ban against communists as such, or Labour-Progressive party members as such, I do not think he could find better words to bar them than those in this clause.
However I do not agree that that is the purpose behind these particular words. These words "Christian and democratic traditions" are the ordinary words used by all ethnic groups in Canada to mean one thing, and that is the Canadian way of life, with the best traditions of their homeland. That is the sense in which the words are used.

Mr. Chairman, I take part in the debate only because of my close association with the branch of the Canadian Slovak League established in St. Catharines. Reference has been made here today to the fact that they might not be loyal to Canadian institutions. In my experience I have found that statement is not correct. I think it is proper that these ethnic groups which come from Europe should bring with them the various crafts, sciences and abilities that they have acquired at home. They have many high qualifications for citizenship which they bring with them. I expect them to have a high degree of loyalty to all Canadian institutions-and they have shown this sense of responsibility. For that reason I believe that many fine citizens who have come to this country and have had good success in business should have the right to incorporate their own Canadian Slovak League to carry on the type of insurance business proposed in the bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all I think it should be made perfectly clear that no one who has taken part in this debate
Private Bills
has expressed any reflection upon the loyalty to Canada or the loyalty to the free institutions of Canada entertained by these people. Too many of us in the House of Commons have connections with them to have any doubts on that score. I think too, Mr. Chairman, it should be said that we all appreciate and agree with the interpretation placed upon these words by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. We recognize that what these people want is to make clear their loyalty to Canada, and to associate with that loyalty the desire to carry forward the best in their own traditions and in their own history.
But it has been made clear time and again that what counts in law is not the interpretation this or that member in the House of Commons may place upon legislation; it is not what is said on the floor of the house that counts, but rather the actual words enacted by parliament. In this instance we are being asked to enact a section which suggests that membership should be open only to those who have (a) loyalty to the free institutions of Canada and (b) loyalty to the Christian and democratic traditions of the Slovak nation.
As other hon. members have said, definitions of "Christian traditions" and definitions of "democratic institutions" vary from one person to another and from one group to another. In this case both those traditions are tied to these words, "the Slovak nation". Well, I do not just know where the Slovak nation is at the present time; it does not exist as a separate nation. If one thinks of part of Czechoslovakia as being the geographical area referred to and as being the historical homeland of these people, then one must face the fact that at the present time that area is under a communist government.
Communist governments talk about their traditions of democratic freedom. There is no doubt that the people named in clause 1 of the bill, the people who have been carrying on this society for many years and who now seek this charter, think of democratic traditions in a quite different vein than is the case with the so-called democratic traditions of that part of Europe at the present time. But if this language is carried forward, then surely one can envisage the possibility of the day coming when people in charge of this society might have a different approach, and might be able to use these very words to exclude certain people or to admit certain others. I submit that we are not splitting hairs here, but are asking for something that we have a right to ask when we suggest that this clause should not carry

Private Bills
a reference to loyalty to certain traditions attaching to a particular nation outside of Canada.
I was pleased to hear the references made by the hon. member for Spadina and the hon. member for Hamilton South when they read from certain other acts. I thought it interesting to listen to those references, and I think they should consider recommending the same language back to those who have requested the passing of this bill. Indeed, I suggest-
I will amend it now, if you sit down.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Good; I shall sit down.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
The hon. member sponsoring the bill has asked me to propose the following amendment:
That clause 5 of the bill be amended by striking out the first three lines thereof down to and including the words "Slovak nation" and substituting therefor:
"Only persons deemed by the society to be of Slovak origin and loyal to the free institutions of Canada and Christian and democratic traditions."

Mr. Chairman, just before the amendment carries I wish to say a few words with reference to the statement made by the hon. member for Nanaimo regarding the great allied statesman, President Tito of Yugoslavia. I have no remarks to make on this particular bill. It seems to me that this amendment strengthens the bill which was introduced in the beginning, but I do think it would be a crying shame if the belittling remark made about the leader of a great friendly nation, whose friendship is being so cultivated by the British commonwealth, President Tito-did I misunderstand my hon. friend?
I think the hon. member for Vancouver South misunderstood my reference. It was not to Tito of Yugoslavia; it was to another person, Father Tizo, you recall, who arose in Czechoslovakia.
Thank you very much; as I heard it over on this side it was "Tito". I was astonished with my hearing, and I am delighted that there is no reflection on President Tito.

I have only a brief remark to make here. I do not think there is any divided loyalty here. The reference to "Christian and democratic traditions of the Slovak nation" refers only to the traditions and not to loyalty to the Slovak nation as such. I should like to say that I do not think there is any doubt in the Slovak mind as to what is meant by reference to Christian and democratic traditions. Before the Slovak nations were overrun by the communists
[Mr. Knowles.l
they did have Christian and democratic governments, and I do not think there is any question in the Slovak mind as to which of the Slovak people have Christian and democratic traditions. I do not think that that particular paragraph will raise any problem of interpretation among the Slovak people. These are the only remarks I wanted to make.

I am very pleased to see that the sponsor of this bill has introduced this amendment. I should like to point out that these organizations come to individual members of parliament and ask them to act as sponsors. I hope that this amendment is in line with what is wanted by the executive officers of the society. I noticed that the previous wording would enable the society to grant membership to people who were not of Slovak origin. The amendment now makes it perfectly clear that the society may grant membership only to people who are of Slovak origin. If that is the wish of the directors I am perfectly happy. However, as the wording was originally-and it may have been deliberately worded that way-it was in order for the society from time to time to give membership to some particular individual who had rendered valuable service to this society or to others.
An important point was raised by the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam. Will the sponsor comment on it?

I have consulted with the
members of the Slovak league on this matter and I told them that possibly I may have to amend this bill. They told me that they concurred in the amendment as I had outlined it to them which I had my hon. friend present to the house. Therefore I believe they are quite satisfied with the amendment as it is. Actually, there is no change in so far as the intent or the meaning of this clause is concerned other than in the explanation. I am quite willing to go along with it, and they are too, and that is to strike out the word "nation". That is the one word which seems to be on everyone's mind. Actually the clause as it originally stood said: only persons deemed by the society to be loyal to the free Institutions of Canada.
And so on. The amendment is: only persons deemed by the society to be of Slovak origin.
It is the same thing, and that wording is quite satisfactory, I am sure, to the sponsors of this bill.

speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Clause as amended agreed to.
Clause 6 agreed to.

On clause 7-Management.

I notice that the affairs of this society are to be managed in this way:
The affairs of the society shall be managed by a board of directors which shall be known as the central assembly and which shall consist of the president, the vice-president, the secretary, the treasurer, the recording secretary, the elder junior branch and five auditors or overseers.
It seems to me a bit odd to have five auditors as members of a board being responsible for management. In most constitutions or bylaws of this sort that I have seen the matter of auditors is attended to by means of a separate sentence saying that the five auditors shall be elected at the annual meeting, or something to that effect. It is very odd to have five members of the board of directors auditing their own financial statements.

I think the intent of that clause really is in the words "and five auditors or overseers". The fact is that they are more or less a board of directors rather than auditors. In a true sense of the word they are auditors, but not in the sense that they are chartered accountants or something of that sort. They are actually overseers rather than auditors. Aside from that fact, I am assured that the superintendent of insurance is quite satisfied with the provisions of the clauses contained in this bill.

I wish I could be a little happier about the statement just made that the superintendent of insurance is perfectly happy about this because it says very definitely that the affairs shall be managed by a board of directors, and it lists them, and then it adds to the board of directors five auditors. I again submit with all due respect that I doubt very much whether this will pass the scrutiny of the superintendent of insurance.

I do not want to disagree with my colleague from Burnaby-Coquitlam, but do not the words "or overseers" give a different meaning to the word "auditors". It is not the same meaning as we give to people who audit the accounts. It is something associated with management rather than with auditing.
That is right.

No property of the society shall, under any circumstances, pass into the private ownership of any

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before clause 1 of this bill carries there are a few words I should like to say. Like a great many of these divorce bills that come before this house this is one which involves a rather tragic story, and a number of elements which I shall refrain from relating on the floor of this house.
I do think, however, that we should take a moment to realize the kind of job we in this parliament are being asked to do. We are here as members of this House of Commons, with members of the other place, to
6022	HOUSE OF
Private Bills-Divorce
pass laws for the general well-being of the people of Canada as a whole, but now we are called upon to use all of our parliamentary machinery for the relief of one individual. That is not to deny the importance of any individual who may be faced with a problem such as this, but I would point out that it was recognized many years ago in the United Kingdom that that was not the function of parliament and it was out of that recognition that divorce courts were first established in the United Kingdom. Parliament's job is to pass laws of general application. Individual problems are best dealt with in courts.
In this case, Mr. Chairman, we have the story of a very young man who was working in the merchant marine. While still under 20 years of age he met a young lady in Glasgow. Apparently they were acquainted with each other for three or four days when they got married. They lived together for about two weeks; then the husband went to sea again. Apparently when he returned to Scotland he discovered that his wife was not living the highest type of life. As a matter of fact, if anyone wishes to read the evidence he will find that the lady in question was guilty of just about everything in the book. At the hearing which was held in the other place the only witness who appeared was the petitioner himself. The respondent, the young woman in question, is still in Scotland and she did not appear.
As I said, there was only one witness, but amongst the exhibits were four sworn affidavits and all these affidavits were received here in Canada from Scotland. Two of them were signed by women who were friends of the wife, one was signed by the wife herself, and the other was signed by a detective. The terms of these affidavits are included in the evidence of this case and they do not make choice reading.
I think hon. members should be made aware that this divorce was granted by Their Honours in the other place on the basis of these affidavits. The petitioner himself was not able to give any direct evidence and he appeared merely to seek a divorce and to answer such questions as were put to him. As I said, the evidence on the basis of which the divorce was granted was based solely on these four signed affidavits. I would point out that the wife in question is perhaps the most damaging witness against herself and her own carryings on for a number of years. In addition to swearing that she is guilty, as I stated, of just about everything in the book, she declares in her affidavit that she is contemplating re-marriage.
Now, no questions were raised, according to the evidence, as to whether there was any


collusion, but it seems pretty clear from that sworn affidavit by the wife that she is quite prepared to give her husband the divorce he wants, and she is prepared to give him this sworn affidavit providing the evidence that is necessary to satisfy Their Honours that a divorce should be granted. She admits in the sworn affidavit that she is contemplating re-marriage which makes it pretty clear that that is perhaps the reason why she is so willing to give that evidence.
So far as the young man himself is concerned, one reads the story as set out in this evidence with a sad heart. One hopes that his future may be better once this situation is in the past so far as he is concerned, and one can even hope that the young woman in question in the married life she contemplates pursuing will have a better future, and that her life will be a better one than it has been in the past.
It might seem to some, Mr. Chairman, that we have no alternative but to agree to a case of this kind, but I have taken these few minutes to spell out the sad details of this case just to impress upon hon. members the obvious fact that this is not the business-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we left off the discussion at five o'clock we were dealing with the amendment and the subamendment which are now before the house. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), the amendment moved by the official opposition is definitely a motion of nonconfidence in the government. As a matter of fact, in wording their amendment I think they took care to make sure that it would be a motion of non-confidence in the government. To that amendment there has been moved by the C.C.F. party in the house an amendment which, by the same token, is also a motion of non-confidence in the government. However, I do not propose to deal with the subamendment on that basis. Rather, I propose to deal with it on its own merits.
I want to say without any hesitation whatever-and I think this will be apparent to all hon. members in this house-that the subamendment moved by the C.C.F. is not realistic, is not sound for the economy of this country and is not in the best interests of the primary producers of this country. As a matter of fact, those in the socialist group who spoke on this subamendment apparently did not have in mind quite clearly what was meant by the mover of the subamendment because there appeared to be some confusion in their minds as to what is meant by floor price and what is meant by parity price.
The hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castle-den), who was the last one to speak, referred to the subamendment merely in the terms of floor price generally. I must admit that I could not figure out why the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough) took the price of $1.82. If the idea was to hold the line, as he put it, it seems to me that it would have been more logical to stick to the $2.05 which had prevailed up until a fairly recent time. On the other hand, I do not think that he could argue that this would constitute a floor, because if it constituted a floor, by the same token, being a higher price than the prevailing market price, it would definitely act as a ceiling as well. It must therefore be viewed in the light of a parity price more than in the light of a floor price.
Naturally, even if we have before us at the moment a motion of non-confidence in the government, I think that members of the opposition also realize that the government at the moment are not trembling in their boots. We know fairly well what the fate of the amendment and the subamendment will be and that it will not change the picture
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus greatly. But since the discussion is, to a large degree, academic, let us suppose that the subamendment were carried by parliament and let us suppose for a moment that parliament instructed the government not to sell any wheat below $1.82. In effect, that is the result of the subamendment. The hon. member who moved the subamendment says that the government is not to sell any wheat below $1.82 or that it is not to pay the producer less than $1.82.
Those are different things.

I will concede the difference. Let us say the amendment is to pay the producer $1.82. As a wheat producer myself, I naturally would have no objection to getting $1.82 instead of $1.72$; and I am quite sure that there is no producer in western Canada who would object to getting $1.82 instead of $1.72$ or less.
How much would you be getting if you were south of the border?
Be patient.

I will come to that particular point.
As so much has been said about the matter I think it is about time that we cleared up this point once and for all. For the moment, as I say, if the government were placed in the position of having to pay the producer $1.82 and no less, it would have to take one of two courses. The first one might be to instruct the wheat board to sell as little wheat as possible since it would have to be sold at a great loss to the taxpayers of the country; and they would take the policy of holding the line, of selling as little as possible, hoping that the price would go up later and they would be able to dispose of the crop. This policy has been tried in the past. It was tried during the thirties. This is exactly the policy that was adopted by the McFarland commission or the McFarland agency in the thirties. We all know what the results of that policy were. Reference was made previously to that point. No one in this house has pronounced himself as being in favour of going back to that policy.
The other course would be to decide to go ahead and to sell wheat at a price higher than the market price and to subsidize the producer. Then naturally it is only common sense that the people of the country would expect the producers to restrict their production. That is an inevitable result.
My hon. friend has just referred to the situation across the border. The situation there is quite different from the one we have

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus here in Canada. As a matter of fact, their position is entirely the reverse of the Canadian position. They consume a large percentage of their production and export a small percentage of it. In Canada we consume a small percentage of our production and export an extremely large percentage of it. Consequently the position in Canada is the reverse of the position in the United States. But in spite of that fact, Mr. Speaker, as you know, last spring the government in the United States had to give an alternative to the producers in the United States. The producers there were given a choice of either accepting a reduction in price or reducing their production. After consultation and conference the farmers, or the representatives of the farmers, agreed to reduce their production, to cut their acreage in wheat rather than to take a cut in price.
In passing may I say this. Let us be clear on what the United States government was attempting to do at the time this parity price system was passed. This system was passed during the war. The purpose of it was definitely to increase the production of wheat in the United States. War conditions existed at that time. They could see that there would be many war-devastated nations in Europe and that there would be a great demand for food products. At that time they did not know how long the war would last. With all these demands they felt that it was in the national interest of the United States and was better policy on the whole to encourage the production of wheat in that nation. Hence they passed what we commonly refer to as the parity price system and agreed to fix the price to the farmer. That price is now $2.21.
This procedure had the desired effect of producing more wheat. Up until the last war the average exports by the United States were roughly in the neighbourhood of 130 million bushels a year. Now their exports are well over 300 million bushels. Hence it will be seen that the desired effect of their policy was attained. I have no quarrel with that procedure. If that is what the American people want to do, it is their business and not ours. However, there is one observation that we make in this country-and we think this is unfortunate-when the rest of the industries of the United States and those in the rest of the world were demobilized, they did not demobilize the wheat industry in their country. The result has been that they have been piling up huge surpluses. As long as they do not dump those surpluses on the markets of the world and do not affect others too drastically, we can have no objection.
[Mr. Jutras.l

Certainly so far they have exercised every care and have shown consideration for their neighbours to the north. We hope that they will continue to consider any move they make in that direction because it would have a very drastic effect on our economy, particularly our agricultural economy. On the other hand, there you are; there is the situation that must be faced. The suggestion contained in the subamendment of the socialists is precisely to adopt a policy with respect to the price of this agricultural commodity that has proved to be a detrimental one in the United States. If it has been so proved in the United States, where their exports are just a small percentage of their total sales, then it is that much more serious and that much more undesirable for a country like Canada where the greater bulk of the product has to be sold outside of this country.
On the face of it the subamendment merely means the freezing of the price of wheat, but we know that it entails a lot more than just the price of wheat. In our western economy wheat is the basic commodity. So it is in the United States. There would be many ramifications. As a matter of fact there is nothing new in the subamendment. This very thing was tried out by the socialists in the United Kingdom when they came into power a few years ago. They initiated a policy of forward fixed prices with the result that they had to exercise control over production, which is inevitable, and after four years the scheme had to be abandoned. I know that the members of the socialist party in particular in this house are well aware of everything that transpired under the socialist government in the United Kingdom. I am sure they are well aware of the very extensive controls and restrictions that the primary producers of the United Kingdom had to put up with. As a matter of fact they were very much opposed to the plan, are still opposed to it and certainly would be opposed to returning to such a system. The national farmers union of the United Kingdom, the largest farm producers organization in that country, has lately come out quite openly and categorically against going back to any such system. They are now directing their efforts towards producer-controlled marketing agencies the same as we have in this country. They have made the experiment in the United Kingdom and it has not proved to be a very successful one.
Here again, let us not forget that in the United Kingdom they do not export any grain. It is entirely a matter of domestic consumption, and consequently the fixing of prices is relatively simple. As a matter of

fact it is very simple. It is the same situation that we have in this country when we control the price of milk in a city. If a province decides to fix the price of milk within the province all it has to do is to pass an order to that effect, and that is being done in many cities across Canada. When the problem is purely domestic you can exercise control over it if you wish, but when a very large part of the product has to be sold in the markets of the world then you have no control whatsoever. You cannot exercise any control over these markets, and that is where the difficulty arises. This is the situation that the United States has to face at the moment.
I know that members of the socialist party have quoted certain farm organizations with the idea of trying to convey the impression that the farmers and primary producers of this country were not aware of these difficulties. Let me refer to the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. In his annual message every year for the last few years he has been warning the producers of the country against any scheme of forward fixed prices, and even against a "parity" system. In his message last year he referred to the United States parity system, and here is what he said:
For twenty years our farmer neighbours to the south of us have had their parity program which did aim to establish profitable prices on the same level as prices and services in the rest of the economy, and then hold them there. Undoubtedly they were partly successful and benefited greatly by it over the period, but today in view of the wide difference of opinion in their own farm ranks, I think it is fair to say that they do not regard it as a complete or adequate answer to maintaining equality and stability for agriculture. And like us, they are looking for a better program. Two of their major organizations are recommending flexible price supports, that is, when production of a particular commodity goes up the floor price will automatically go down and vice versa.
I think it will be apparent that any scheme of fixed prices must of necessity be related in some degree at least to the production because we fall into the other difficulties that I have mentioned. Again in the month of January this year the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture had this to say in his annual message:
That a support program based on a high percentage of "parity" is not the best answer is indicated by experience in the United States and by changes which are being insisted upon there by both the producers and the government. When a program of forward fixed prices with practically all phases of the farm economy controlled is now being abandoned in the United Kingdom, it may indicate at least that that is not likely to be the one that we would want to try in Canada. Incidentally, in their efforts to replace that program the national farmers' union are placing most emphasis on orderly regulated marketing under producer boards.
15, 1954
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus
I think that even my hon. friends of the C.C.F. party will agree that all in all this represents pretty well the thinking of the primary producers of this country. The emphasis today is placed upon primary producers' marketing boards or agencies rather than freezing prices at any level, particularly any unrealistic level.
When the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) spoke he made some very drastic and farfetched statements. I do not propose to deal with every one of them because my time will not allow. However, there is one that he made repeatedly and which was repeated by some of his colleagues several times, not to mention the hon. member for Yorkton who preceded me. I should like to quote this one sentence which illustrates pretty well the thought running through the minds of the socialist group in this discussion. He made the flat statement that "the Canadian government has always opposed the principle of floor prices and the principle of orderly marketing". This was repeated by him and repeated by other members of his group.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as you and every hon. member of the house knows, the present government is probably the government of Canada that has done the most in the history of the nation to encourage orderly marketing for the primary producers. I think every primary producer and every farmer in western Canada knows that. Exercising some measure of control over marketing is not new. As a matter of fact it goes back to pre-confederation days. But the present government that is now in office, and probably to some degree because it has been so long in office, has certainly done more than any other government in the history of the nation for primary producers of this country. When that statement by the hon. member is made particularly in relation to the marketing of wheat, then it is so far away from the truth you wonder if the hon. member was not carried away by the enthusiasm of the moment. However, we cannot say that because he repeated it two or three times during his speech.
I am not going to enter a debate as to who should get the most credit for establishing the Canadian wheat board. I concede quite readily, and I am quite happy to be able to do so, that it came into existence three months before the government of the Hon. R. B. Bennett was dissolved. I believe every fair-minded member will agree that it was under the present administration that the Canadian wheat board was made the strong marketing agency it is today. It was not
6026	HOUSE OF
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus done because the government was opposed, it was done because the government did everything to encourage it and make it possible for the board to be what it is today. Nobody can deny that fact. All hon. members in this house, without exception, agree that it is the best marketing agency we could possibly have in this country. I have never met anyone in this house that dared challenge this statement.
As was pointed out before, and apparently will have to be pointed out again, it was only a few weeks ago that the annual report of the Canadian wheat board came before the standing committee on agriculture and colonization. The three commissioners of the Canadian wheat board were before the committee and everyone was at liberty to question them as much as they liked. As a matter of fact the committee went through the whole operation of the board and everyone asked the questions they wished. The commissioners were quite willing to answer all the questions. I thought the whole matter had been gone into thoroughly. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) made the statement that no one objected, and I defy anyone to go through the records of the committee and find anyone who dissented from what the board was doing. Everyone agreed that this was the best possible way of doing it.
The socialist members even went so far as to put a direct question to the chairman of the Canadian wheat board, asking him if he thought this was the best way of doing it. Naturally, being the chairman of the board, it could not be expected that he would say anything else, but for the purpose of the record he did say that naturally he thought this was the best way of doing it. The hon. member for Assiniboia was quite as enthusiastic in agreeing with the chairman, and is on the record as saying, "Very good; very good". When a suggestion was made about the other method of marketing and they asked the chairman if he thought this was not a better method, naturally the answer was that the present one was a better method.
This afternoon the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) tried to indicate that he at least, if nobody else, had offered some criticism of the board. I must say that if he had criticism in mind he did not make it quite clear because I am sure he was the only one who thought he made any serious criticism of the marketing system.

I believe, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should make a correction here. I was making my criticism in the agriculture committee and in this house to a large extent of
[Mr. Jutras.l

the policy of the government. I was not criticizing the board, because they have to do what they are told.

I should like to point out to the hon. member for Calgary North that for the moment I am not referring to the policy of the government. I am referring to the operations of the board, and for the moment I am restricting my remarks to the actual operation. I shall come to the policy level later. So far as the board is concerned, and so far as their sales of wheat are concerned, there has been no serious criticism. This afternoon the hon. member referred to actual sales of the last three or four months. This question was also put in the committee, as he knows-
No, no.
I will give the hon. member the page reference after I am through.
Not after January 31 of this year.

No, but up until January. The hon. member tried to make the same point in the committee, and the clear statement of the chairman of the board is on the record to the effect that it is useless to take one week, two weeks or one month in the marketing year as giving any possible indication of the year's operations. We can see from last year's report that there was a period in which there was no marketing. Members of the committee asked why that was so, and were told that at that time there happened to be a strike. There was no grain moving. There might be almost any situation occurring at a particular moment. There are many factors affecting marketing such as weather, transportation and many others. Picking out any one week or one month or two months cannot possibly give any indication of the year's operation.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) also made a statement, and prefaced his remarks by saying that none of the last crop was sold. That is quite true; I mean it is in a way of speaking. Last year there was as much wheat left over as the entire crop, so we could say that none of the wheat was sold during that year. Standing alone that is a misleading statement because in the same year we exported more wheat than we ever exported in the entire history of the nation. We established an all time high record for selling wheat outside of this nation.
That is the previous year you are talking about.
No, the same crop year, 1952-53.
That is the previous year.

speechtext:
Yes, and that all comes back to the fact that we have had three very large crops in western Canada during the last three years.
Some hon. members have tried to create the impression that we have lost our markets. The chairman of the wheat board was asked that question and he made the categorical statement that we had not lost any of our markets. It was just that the percentage went down. This was attributed to the fact that the United Kingdom is not buying but is using up her stockpile. There are many nations in Europe which were buying wheat before who have had such good crops they are now selling wheat. The United States has boosted its production, and we have had large crops. Naturally, therefore, there is a large amount of wheat on the market at the moment.
I see my time is running out, and I should like to deal with another important statement. I must say I regret the fact the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) is not in his seat. No doubt he has been detained by important business. I am not saying anything to reflect on him in that regard, but since I want to deal with remarks he made it makes it a little difficult when he is not in the house. However, a few days ago when he moved a motion to adjourn the house he gave a statement to the press which I felt was very unfortunate and should be dealt with now. I am quoting from an article in the Ottawa Citizen of Tuesday, June 8, which says:
Mr. Diefenbaker, who told reporters the price drop is a blow to the western farmer, blamed it largely on Canada's stubborn refusal to agree to Britain's request for a ceiling of $2 a bushel instead of $2.05 under the international wheat agreement.
The hon. member for Prince Albert should definitely know the situation in this regard, and should know that this is not accurate.
Well, you see how these things snowball. Two days later a very reputable newspaper, the Montreal Gazette, carried an editorial commenting on this situation and taking that as a matter of fact in writing the editorial. Then again, a few days ago, some private citizens in Ottawa wrote a letter to the editor along the same lines which appeared on the editorial page.
To begin with, the hon. member for Prince Albert says that he blames it on the stubborn refusal to agree to Great Britain's request for a ceiling of $2. I have not time to place all the information on the record, but the first inference there is that he has always taken the position that we should have agreed to a price lower than $2.05. All we have to do is to read the pages of Hansard, at
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus the time we ratified the agreement, to find that the hon. member for Prince Albert was the one who inferred, I believe on four occasions, that the price was not high enough. But he went further than that. Here is what the hon. member said on this matter of the price range:
With increasing farm costs, a price level such as that suggested in today's Canadian Press article-
Referring to the suggestion that it might be $2.
-will, I think, be most detrimental to the wheat producer of this country on the basis of the suggested maximum and minimum prices set forth in that article.
And in the course of these remarks he went on further and suggested that-
-the Minister of Trade and Commerce would give consideration to asking the purchasing countries to accept some escalator clause whereby, in the event of increasing farm costs, there would be increases in the minimum price.
Not only was he against the $2 price, but he wanted to tie an escalator clause to it. The idea was to force purchasing nations to be tied to the escalator clause on top of that. And yet today he turns around and says that he blames it all largely on Canada's stubborn refusal to agree to $2. That is the first inference.
Then, the second inference is that it was Canada who held out definitely for $2.05. Well, we all know the facts of the situation. That was over a year ago. When the negotiating team got down to the last stages the United Kingdom suggested price was $1.95. The Americans had started at $2.50, and it was made clear by the United States delegates that they could not possibly recommend anything below $2, that it would not have a chance of carrying in congress, and that consequently they could not consider anything below $2. They said that $2.05, which looked a little more than $2, was the best they could do; and they had to negotiate on that basis.
I would not put the blame on the United States more than on any other country. But at that time both the producers in the United States and in this country felt very strongly that $2.05 was the limit in North America, and we agreed to that. I am willing to take my responsibility for that, the same as anybody else. I am not trying to say that we should have agreed; but we have the statement of the chairman of the Canadian wheat board before the committee. When he was asked if he thought we could sell more wheat by taking less for it, or if he felt we could have sold more at a lower price, he made the very definite statement, without any hesitation at all, that it would not have made
6028	HOUSE OF
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus any difference. It was not a question of price; it was just a question that they did not want to buy. He pointed out that 5 cents, 10 cents or 15 cents would not have made any difference. And he was quite categorical on the point that price at that time and up until now has not been a feature in the lower sales in the international market.
So that this argument that the present reduced price is the outcome of the negotiations at the time of the international wheat agreement is not valid. And I want to place on record again that I hope members of the official opposition will not try to repeat what they tried to do after the British wheat agreement. They never would concede, but they had agreed to the British wheat agreement. Then a few years later they tried to deny they had ever supported the British wheat agreement. All parties in the house, without exception, supported the international wheat agreement and supported the terms of it to the same extent. Some of them would have preferred, the same as we would have, some other provisions; but the fact remains that we all agreed to support this agreement because those were the best terms we could get.
The situation developing now is a situation of overproduction, and it is not one that has anything to do with whatever price was arrived at, at the international level. And I might add personally I feel very strongly that during the years it has been in operation it has served a very useful purpose, and it is still serving a very useful purpose. Because we have been able to agree to some degree.
I agree fully with the Minister of Trade and Commerce that it is far better policy to take a package drop, rather than to allow the price to drop a half cent, a cent or two cents at a time. It might well develop into a price war at the international level. And at least this is a fact, that a package drop at one time has the effect of holding it there. And I for one-and I am sure this is shared by the Minister of Trade and Commerce- hope that it will not develop into something more.
I want to say in conclusion that while the opposition has been complaining so much that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is an optimist, I am very gratified and pleased that he is an optimist. We are very fortunate in that, because it is much preferable to have an optimist in that position. Of all people, I cannot understand primary producers complaining about the fact that they have an optimist in that position. After all, for one thing, in a few weeks' time he will have to set the initial price. I hope he will
[Mr. Jutras.l

be very optimistic in the future outlook when he sets the initial price, and will set it as an optimist, rather than as a pessimist.

Mr. Speaker, the reasons for supporting the amendment introduced this morning by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) were fully set out by him in his excellent speech. It becomes necessary, however, to make a brief statement concerning our position in regard to the C.C.F. subamendment.
Let me say at the outset that the matter of the marketing of Canadian wheat is a subject of importance to every Canadian. Its importance is not confined to the western provinces, nor to those who represent the western provinces. The finding of good markets for Canadian wheat, our principal food export, is something basic to the whole Canadian economy; and it is with an appreciation of that fact that I approach the problem now.
The government has monopolistic powers over the disposal of wheat in Canada. Therefore it must accept full responsibility for whatever may be lacking in the disposal of Canadian wheat. I sought in my remarks last week to indicate the reasons why the Canadian people and members of the House of Commons expect that the government, in the discharge of its responsibilities as the salesman of Canadian wheat, must be an energetic and resourceful salesman. As indicated in our amendment we think the government has failed. It has not measured up to its responsibilities as the salesman of Canadian wheat.
I am not going to weary the house with figures. I will give the house only the more recent evidence. It is true that our wheat marketings in the crop year 1952-53 were something of a record, totalling approximately 378 million bushels. Up to May 15 of the present crop year 1953-54 our total exports were only 196 million bushels. In other words, in the first 9J months of the present crop year we have marketed barely one-half of the marketings in the previous crop year, and it will take a mighty spurt in the remaining 2J months of the crop year after May 15 to make any impression at all in reducing this huge disparity between the marketings of the year 1952-53 and the greatly reduced market ings of the year 1953-54.
The United Kingdom is our best customer for wheat. What then have been our marketings in the United Kingdom in those two crop years? In the crop year 1952-53 we marketed 123 [DOT] 4 million bushels of wheat in wheat and wheat flour in the United Kingdom. Up to the end of April, 1954, in other words, in

nine months of the present crop year, Canada had marketed in the United Kingdom only 59 million bushels of wheat in wheat and wheat flour. In other words, in the first nine months of this crop year we did not market as much as half of our marketings in the United Kingdom in the full crop year 1952-53, and that is a fact that must fill us all with very grave concern.
Canada has on hand now approximately 675 million bushels of wheat. World stocks at May 1 aggregated 1,800 million bushels in the four major exporting countries, the United States, Canada, Australia and Argentina. Of that huge total, one-half was located in the United States. Measure that stock of wheat, Mr. Speaker, at May 1, this year, 1,800 million bushels, with the situation exactly one year earlier, when the total world stock in those four great exporting countries was just 1,338 million bushels.
The alarming feature of the way in which the government demonstrates its attitude towards this problem is that so far as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), as the spokesman of the government, is concerned, he apparently does not see a problem in it. He seems to be quite content with what we are doing. He does not recognize the existence of a problem. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the minimum essential, the first requirement of the solution of any problem is that we should recognize the existence of the problem, and there is scant hope of effective solution of this problem, which is a problem for all Canadians, as long as the government through the Minister of Trade and Commerce is content to deny even the existence of a problem.
After all the government's promises, and after all its bragging, and after all the kidding that it has practised at the expense of the western wheat farmer, we see a situation here today which ought to be giving great concern to hon. members, and it is for that reason that the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) moved this amendment in which we invite the house to express its concern over this problem in these words:
This house regrets that the government has failed to deal effectively with the problem of marketing Canada's wheat surplus.
I now turn to the C.C.F. subamendment which reads as follows:
That the amendment be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma and by adding thereafter the following words:
"and this house further regrets that the government has failed to make provision for a floor price to the wheat producers of Canada at levels not less than the Canadian wheat board selling price, basis Fort William/Port Arthur, on Friday. June 4, 1954."
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus Sir, as has been indicated, that price was $1.82J per bushel. Since the date referred to in the subamendment the government has reduced the price of wheat by 10 cents a bushel, and if one is to follow the statement made by the minister in the course of this debate more reductions are threatened.
May I recall what the minister said in the course of this debate on June 9 at page 5750 of Hansard?
If it is necessary to cut the price again in order to hold that proportion, I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we are not going to lose markets for wheat because we make a fetish of $1,781 for Vancouver and $1,721 for Fort William and, by making a fetish, lose markets for substantial quantities of wheat.
And again, speaking of our customers among the countries of the world, he said on the same page:
If they are not buying from us when our turn comes, we make inquiries to find out why. If it is a matter of price, that is one factor which, added to other factors, may indicate to the wheat board that a cut in price is necessary.
Those are the facts of life. That is the policy that the wheat board will follow. It is the purpose of the board to be competitive.
There is only one interpretation that these words bear, and that is an intimation from the minister that the Canadian wheat farmer may expect further reductions in the price of his products.
Now I turn to this subamendment and I ask where would the adoption of the kind of policy outlined in the C.C.F. subamendment lead us as a nation? What might it cost to implement this policy? It is quite true that this subamendment, calling for the expenditure of money, cannot commit parliament to the expenditure itself, but nevertheless we are called upon in the forthcoming division on this subamendment to express ourselves in relation to that policy. I ask in the first place: What would the policy cost? I measure it against the background in which the present government has not been very successful in selling wheat. I point out that the subamendment is not confined to wheat of the 1953-54 crop year. Apparently it is intended to be the continuing policy, assuring a floor of $1.82J per bushel on all wheat grown or marketed hereafter, or after June 4.
We have on hand, as I indicated earlier, approximately 675 million bushels of wheat just six weeks now from the commencement of the next crop year. Add the crop year 1954-55 to our stock on hand today of approximately 675 million bushels and it will be seen that the policy indicated in the C.C.F. subamendment is going to have an application to a great deal of wheat in the next year or two. Let us take it both ways. Let us assume on

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus the one hand that we may have a much reduced crop in the next crop year. Let us say, for instance, that the crop in the crop year 1954-55 is just 325 million bushels. Let us assume on the other hand, for purposes of calculation, that Canada has for the fourth year in succession a bumper crop of 625 million bushels. Add these respective quantities of 325 million bushels on the one hand and 625 million bushels on the other to our existing stock of approximately 675 million bushels and it will be seen that if we have a poor crop in the crop year 1954-55 this policy will apply to approximately one billion bushels of wheat. On the other hand, if we have another big crop year in Canada in the crop year 1954-55 this policy will apply between now and the end of the crop year 1954-55 to some 1,300 million bushels of wheat.
In measuring the cost let us regard also the rather chilling warning given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the passage which I have just quoted as to the expectation of further reductions in the price of wheat. Here is the way in which these figures of cost work out. If the present price of $1.72 per bushel continues this policy would cost the Canadian taxpayer 10 cents per bushel. If we have one billion bushels of wheat to market in terms of the present quantity and next year's crop, this will cost the Canadian taxpayer $100 million. On the other hand, if we have the large crop I mentioned and we have to dispose of 1,300 million bushels of wheat then it would cost the Canadian taxpayer $130 million to implement this policy.
Now suppose this chilling news given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce issues in a further reduction and we assume the next reduction is to $1.62J per bushel. The Canadian taxpayer must then subsidize every bushel of wheat to the extent of 20 cents and in that event to dispose of one billion bushels of wheat the cost to the Canadian taxpayer would be $200 million. On the other hand, if we have the big crop to dispose of amounting to 1,300 million bushels the cost to the Canadian taxpayer would be $260 million.
If the Minister of Trade and Commerce pursues further the policy of which he gave us that chilling warning last week and let us say the price at which the government proposes to sell the wheat drops another 10 cents per bushel to $1.52J per bushel, this time it will mean that the Canadian taxpayer will be required to subsidize every bushel of wheat to the extent of 30 cents, and if we have one billion bushels of wheat to dispose of the bill to the Canadian taxpayer will be 

$300 million. If we have to dispose of 1,300 million bushels of wheat the bill to the Canadian taxpayer will be $390 million.

There is the Minister of Trade and Commerce apparently seriously suggesting that there is the possibility of some further drop. I say to the minister that if this is the best consideration he can offer he had better get off the job and make way for somebody who will do a better job of selling Canadian wheat at proper prices.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Try eating a little more wheat.

The fact of the matter is that to implement this policy no one here can tell where it would lead. It is laid down as a policy of continuous application. The quantities of which I have spoken include only the stock on hand today plus the crop for the crop year 1954-55. It is quite evident that no one in this house knows what the continuing cost of this policy would be. It is, however, not to be wondered at that hon. members introduce an amendment of this kind, particularly when we see the fruits of the government's failure in the way in which it has misled the western farmer by all the airy talk it has offered to the wheat farmers of the west for years past, but in the face of the facts I have put before the house, and the fact that no one knows where a plunge of this kind would take us, we in this part of the house cannot give support to the C.C.F. subamendment.
I do not wish to close my remarks this evening without laying all the emphasis at my command on one thing. I conceive it to be the duty of the government in fairness to western wheat farmers immediately to do something that the government has been asked repeatedly to do, particularly today in the speech made by my esteemed colleague the hon. member for Calgary North. It is the duty of this government immediately to announce the initial payment on the 1954-55 crop. Never in all the years since the conclusion of the five-year wheat pool has the government been so late and so tardy in announcing the initial payment on the new crop. We are now at June 15. I suggest we take a look at the dates on which the initial payment was announced during the previous four years. For the crop year 1950-51 the

government announced the initial payment on April 5, 1950. This is just 71 days earlier than the day on which we are meeting here now. For the crop year 1951-52 the government announced the initial payment on May 4, 1951, 42 days in advance of June 15. For the crop year 1952-53 the government announced the initial payment on April 8, 1952, just 68 days ahead of June 15. For the crop year 1953-54 the government announced the initial payment on April 27, 1953, just 49 days ahead of June 15.
Never throughout this entire period, has the government been anything like so late as this year. Now, sir, this is a matter of the liveliest concern to the western wheat growers. It is a matter of lively concern to others as well. It is a matter of concern to "the butcher, the baker, the candlestick maker" in western Canada and elsewhere. It is a matter of concern to the railways and indeed to the entire country.
Why has the government been so coy about announcing the initial price? Why this tardiness? There was a statement from the minister in his speech on this matter in this house on June 9 which, if not explained by the minister, can only be described as misleading. The minister said, as reported at page 5746 of Hansard for June 9:
The present-
Note these words, Mr. Speaker.
-initial price has been $1.40 basis No. 1 northern for several years, and that is the initial price today. It has been said here that there is no floor under wheat. What more effective floor can there be than an outstanding offer to pay on the basis of $1.40 at terminal delivery point when wheat is delivered at the country elevator?
At the risk of repetition, Mr. Speaker, I would again draw your attention to the words the minister used in reference to "the present initial price of $1.40". He says that that is the initial price today. But the fact of the matter is that that was the initial price for the crop year 1953-54, and that price was announced on April 27, 1953, nearly 14 months ago.
No announcement has been made, and none has been attempted on the part of the government as to the initial payment for the crop year 1954-55, which is the crop year that is giving the farmer immediate concern as to what the initial payment will be. Of course, he knows what initial payment was received for the crop year 1953-54; he has known that for the last 14 months.
It is surely not necessary for the minister to make statements of that kind which, without explanation on his part, it seems to me can only mislead those who read them.
