We are now only six weeks away from the beginning of a new crop year. No one knows what to expect. Government policy is an enigma. If the government has not a policy, then it is time they found one and found it soon, in simple justice to the Canadian wheat farmer and to all those Canadians who depend upon the Canadian wheat farmer for the success and the economic health of their efforts. I say that it would be the gravest injustice if the government defers for one moment longer announcing an initial price for the crop year 1954-55.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate which has been going on with regard to the marketing of wheat during two complete days now is one which always creates a certain amount of interest in the house. This debate is no exception. There is, however, one matter which I do not think has much bearing upon the question which is before the house. Nevertheless it has been referred to in the speeches of two different members, namely the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) and the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch). I may say that this is not the first occasion upon which it has been referred to.
Since there has been considerable argument about it, I am sure that you will permit me to deal with it for a few moments. It has been suggested by both hon. members that on some occasion I voted against an international commodity clearing house as proposed by the farm federation. On previous occasions I had not taken the trouble to look up the record to see whether or not I had voted against it. I knew exactly what I had said on the occasion when the question was under discussion. I did not recall ever having voted at all upon it one way or the other. This afternoon, when the question was raised on the other side of the house, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) stated that the real question is this: Did you vote against it? I hope I can answer that question to his satisfaction tonight.
I have read through the debate which was referred to this afternoon by the hon. member for Acadia. He referred back to a debate which we had in this house on April 30, 1953, upon the same question. Practically everything that has been said both inside and outside of the house with regard to this matter is based upon what the hon. member for Acadia said and on what he induced me to say. I am not going to hold him any more responsible for what was said than I am going to hold myself. The suggestion was made time after time that I had voted against

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus the international policy as suggested by Sir John Boyd Orr. I made it quite plain that I had not done so. As a matter of fact, my speeches at all the international conferences on food and agriculture will bear me out when I say that I was always one of the chief supporters of the policy whenever it was brought up for discussion at any of the FAO conferences. That is all I am going to say about that matter.
My hon. friend from Acadia was good enough to point out in the speech of April 30, 1953 that he quite agreed that I supported Sir John Boyd Orr's international proposals. The hon. member for Assiniboia the other day did not accept that point of view at all, and he was quoting from the speech of the hon. member for Acadia. He was saying that I did not support that position. I want to thank the hon. member for Acadia for putting him right this afternoon-at least he will be put right when he reads Hansard because he was not here at the time and is not here now-by saying again that he acknowledged the fact that I had always supported that policy. But he said that I or the Canadian delegation of which I was the head had voted against this international commodity clearing house that was proposed.
I must say that where I was led a little bit astray was that after I took a column or two of Hansard on that occasion to explain just exactly what I did say down there, I said this; and this is the only sentence out of the whole discussion that the hon. member for Acadia saw fit to read this afternoon-
That is all that is necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We will find out in a few
moments whether or not it is all that is necessary. I had not expected that from the hon. member for Acadia. I endorse everything that the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) said this afternoon wtih regard to the members of the other group who continuously take positions of that kind, not because they are in accordance with the facts but simply because they serve the purpose for the time being.
My hon. friend, out of all this speech- and in this I explain exactly why the Canadian delegation took certain positions with regard to the matter-read this one sentence:
If we went into a scheme of that kind with a group of nations that would not accept the principles that were laid down by Lord Orr, then of course we would be looking for trouble;-

-so we voted against it.

That is a good thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

Nevertheless I had never looked up the records until this afternoon. I looked them up and I have them here. As a matter of fact, no vote at all was taken on the question. The only reasons there were for the Canadian delegation taking the position it took are explained in the speech which I made. In that speech nothing at all is said about a vote and it does not touch upon a vote, for the simple reason that results were obtained in another way. I am going to read only the last two sentences of the speech which I delivered on that occasion. They will make it plain why I examined the records in order to find out whether or not there had ever been a vote.
Unless the proposed international agency, with the co-operation of the governments concerned, could direct the disposal of any substantial surpluses which may arise in a way that would avoid this kind of development, then the effort of other exporting countries to maintain production levels in keeping with natural demand would be jeopardized and far-reaching effects might result throughout the entire food and agriculture economy of the world.
Then the last sentences:
In conclusion, we in Canada agree with the United States and the United Kingdom that suggestions should be considered by a working committee. The Canadian delegation will co-operate in every possible way on such a committee. We hope that out of this conference will come a suggestion that we can all agree on.
Following that a working committee was set up and the conference had sufficient confidence in the Canadian delegation to place the deputy minister of agriculture of that day from this country-I refer to Dr. Barton -at the head of the committee. That commodity committee of the FAO organization sat throughout the years in order to arrive at some suitable method of handling this question of surpluses of farm products throughout the world.
Well now, I wish to repeat again that according to the statements of the officials who were there, and I checked with some of them this afternoon, there was no vote taken on this question at all. The question that was before the conference was fully discussed. Our opinion with regard to it was clearly expressed and following that, not only because of the position we took but because of the position others at that conference took, a committee was set up to go to work on the matter of international surpluses in order to determine the best possible way of dealing with them from year to year. That committee sat and carried out its activities throughout the years.
I wanted to say that on this occasion because I know why my hon. friends keep repeating these things. They do so for the

very reason expressed by both of the hon. members, although one of them is in the C.C.F. group and the other in the Social Credit group. They say: Well, we cannot rely on your statements anyway. Of course, every time they can put anything on the record which makes it appear that my statement is not exactly correct they feel that helps them in some way in creating just the kind of impression that the hon. member for Rosthern said this afternoon they were bent upon creating with regard to anyone in this house who differs with their opinion.

Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I do not think the minister has any right to suggest that I made that statement purely to infer that the minister was making an incorrect statement. I did so for the simple reason that I wanted to find out what the attitude of the government was, and I referred the minister to the statement he made last year in which he said that he had voted against the proposal. I have seen reports of that conference which state that the conference turned down the proposal. In view of the fact that the government of which the minister is a member is opposed to the acceptance of sterling, and in view of the fact that the international commodity clearing house is based upon the acceptance of sterling, I do not see how the minister could possibly have done anything else than oppose the proposal.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is all right. I do not think my hon. friend needs to make another speech. He raised the question whether or not I was inferring something that I should not infer. Because the minister kept changing his statement.

In view of the fact that this matter has been dealt with on a number of occasions I thought it necessary for me to make a statement once again and to put the position clearly on record.
Coming back to the question which we have before us at the moment, which is an important one. It has been said by hon. members that we should follow the American practice at the present time in connection with the handling of wheat. I have the American plan here in my hand, and having it in my hand I think I should place it on the record. These are the acreage allotments and marketing quotas on United States wheat.
1.	Authority for acreage allotments and marketing quotas is provided in the agricultural adjustment act of 1938 as amended. This legislation provides that not later than July 15 of each marketing year for wheat the secretary shall ascertain and proclaim the total supply and the normal supply of wheat for such marketing year and the national acreage allotment for the next crop of wheat. It provides further that when the secretary determines that the supply of wheat will exceed a certain quantity, as set out in section 335(a), he shall, not later than July 1, proclaim the fact and that during the marketing year beginning July 1 of the next succeeding calendar year a marketing quota shall be in effect. Between the date of issuance of such proclamation and July 25-mid-August in the amended legislation-a referendum is to be held to determine whether the farmers approve the quota. If more than one-third of the farmers oppose it the secretary shall by proclamation suspend the operation of the quota.
That is the first provision in connection with the establishment of support for wheat prices in the United States.
Then I come to the next one.
2.	The agricultural act of 1949 provides price support for wheat at 90 per cent of parity for cooperators, defined as those whose acreage does not exceed the farm acreage allotment-
In other words, just as the chairman of the agricultural committee said a few moments ago in discussing this question, when you impose price controls and establish anything in the nature of what they have in the United States you must have along with it acreage control as well. The two things are tied together.
The agricultural act of 1949 provides price support for wheat at 90 per cent of parity for co-operators-defined as those whose acreage does not exceed the farm acreage allotment-if the marketing quotas have not been disapproved. The rate is to be 50 per cent of parity for co-operators if the marketing quotas have been disapproved by producers.

That is quite a different proposition from the proposition that has been discussed here.
It has been suggested that the farmer in the United States goes ahead and produces whatever wheat he feels inclined to produce; that that wheat is produced at 90 per cent of parity; that a loan is made upon it to the extent of 90 per cent of parity, and then he can do so and so and so and so. That is not correct at all.

Who made that
statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The fact of the matter is that if 90 per cent of parity is established by the vote that takes place once a year the individual is bound by that acreage once it is established. If he has any more than that amount of acreage seeded then the amount he is allowed, if he is allowed anything at all, is considerably less that 90 per cent on all the wheat he grew.
Then I come to the third point.
3.	The national acreage allotment under the existing legislation is to be such that with normal yields and taking into account estimated carry-over and imports it will make available an amount equal to a normal year's domestic consumption and exports, plus 30 per cent thereof. The minimum for any year was to be not less than 55 million acres.
In other words, the acreage in the United States, which at the end of the war was 83 million acres, could be reduced to 55 million acres. As everyone knows, when the vote was taken last August the acreage in the United States was reduced by 16 million acres. That 16 million acres taken off the 78 million made an acreage of 62 million. The fact is that if American farmers seed more than their quota of the 62 million acres then those who exceed their quota in acres will, under this particular proposal, suffer thereby in so far as any support for prices they get is concerned.
How much a bushel for his wheat, though?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I might say to the hon. member for Mackenzie that I once heard a very prominent member in this house make the remark that no one ever listens himself into trouble.
4.	The prospective supply for the 1954 crop year was such that this minimum would have been in effect. Amending legislation signed by the President on July 14, 1953 set the 1954 allotment at 62 million acres-
-the figure which I gave a moment ago. The 1953 wheat acreage was 78 million acres.

5.	The referendum on the wheat marketing quota for 1954 was held on August 14, 1953. The quota was approved, over 87 per cent of the farmers voting in favour of it.
As the hon. chairman of the agricultural committee said a few moments ago, you cannot tie down the price of wheat and make that work successfully unless at the same time you have acreage control. If there is one thing that the western farmers have voted against, talked against and worked against ever since I have been in Saskatchewan, and that is ever since the province was formed, it has been any kind of acreage control. Of course the reason for that is obvious. We are a new province. Farmers are settling here and there throughout the length and breadth of it. They have objected at all times to acreage control, and because they have objected to acreage control many of the things that are being suggested from the other side of the house are an impossibility.
A few moments ago something was said by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) about the supplies of wheat that have been sold at different times. Prior to the war Britain was very anxious that she should not be put into the position where she was consuming more than 90 million bushels of our wheat in a year. This did not mean that she would not buy any more than 90 million bushels of our wheat. There was a time when Britain bought wheat for the most of Europe. She bought it from us and other people and distributed it to the countries in Europe. Since the war she has not felt in a position to do that kind of thing, so she has been buying wheat for herself and allowing others to make arrangements for the supplies they required.
I have here a table of the imports of wheat into the United Kingdom from the different countries during 1951, 1952 and 1953. I shall just use the round figures, because it is only to get comparisons. Australia exported to the United Kingdom in 1951, 21 million bushels; in 1952, 16 million bushels; in 1953, 14 million bushels. Canada exported in 1951 just four times what Australia placed in the United Kingdom, 84 million bushels; in 1952, 103 million bushels; in 1953, for nine months -this statement just carries me down to the end of September-83 million bushels. These are calendar years, not crop years. Then from the United States the United Kingdom imported in 1951, 39 million bushels; then 16 million and 16 million, for the next two years. The figures for France are as follows: 1,200,000; 797,000; 12,500. The figures for other countries are 5,293,000;	681,000;

1,618,000. The Soviet union supplied wheat only in one year out of that group, the year 1952, 7,338,000 bushels.
Now, let me call attention again to the sales Canada made. They were, in 1951, 84 million bushels; in 1952, 103 million bushels, and in the first nine months of 1953, 83 million bushels. I have the figures for flour here, and when you take in flour and wheat the figure is raised to the figures mentioned a few moments ago by the hon. member for Eglinton for 1952 of 123 million bushels. When you take wheat and flour both, the other figures are comparable.
What I wanted to point out was this. Britain has been taking about the usual amounts of wheat and flour from this country. When you take the first year, for example, the figures are 84 million bushels of wheat and 9 million bushels in the form of flour. For the next year, there is a similar position and in the last year it is 83 million bushels of wheat for nine months and 6 million bushels in the form of flour. The figures work out to be quite comparable but are much higher than any other country sold to Britain.
When my hon. friends opposite are discussing this question, I should like to point out that one cannot be too sure what these figures mean. Britain is a very careful trader. Britain is concerned about seeing her population is fed, in a country where they cannot produce more than about 50 per cent of their own food, and so she does her own storing in her own way. When there is a situation that may threaten war, she has her own methods of storing up and retaining certain amounts until she is sure there is not going to be any trouble, or comparatively sure that there is not. She then consumes the wheat in storage and buys less.
There is not any way in which anyone in this house can take these matters and consider them reasonably in any other manner than by taking a long period of time. To say that Britain only bought so much wheat in some months or some particular year is on the face of it ridiculous if you want to make comparisons. Even saying that Britain only took so much wheat in a particular year, particularly if you can show an unusually high amount in the preceding year, does not mean that one is at all sure whether she is supplying the nation in that year or whether she is supplying storages to take care of any difficulties which may happen in the next year.
What we in this country, and those in every other country that is selling wheat in the markets over there, must do is to do our own reasoning. We must come to our own conclusion and go ahead from whatever
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus point of view we reach. We must do the best we possibly can in support of our own people who are producing the product, and that is exactly what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been doing, in so far as he directs the wheat board at all. I know from long experience in dealing with the wheat board that no one here directs the wheat board. The wheat board comes here from time to time and asks for advice on certain things they may wonder whether or not they should do. As for the minister directing them as to what they should do, that board was set up at the request of the producers in western Canada and at the request of no one else. It took the producers years to establish the idea here. First they tried it with the preceding government, and I believe there is only one member in this house now who was in that government then. The farmers attempted to have the preceding government establish a compulsory wheat board. They put forth every effort to have that done.
I must say, to the credit of the Bennett government of that day, that they brought down a bill which provided not only for compulsory marketing of wheat but compulsory marketing of all grain. My friend shakes his head, but I say to him to go and read the legislation.
I was just shaking my head because it is a red letter day when a fair remark is made from across the gangway about the Bennett government.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I beg my hon. friend's
pardon for having thought anything else. In so far as the statement is concerned, I have said it so often without getting credit for it that I am sure I appreciate the credit I get tonight. The government of Mr. Bennett brought down a bill to provide for the compulsory marketing of western grain through a wheat board. There was a discussion about it on the floor of the house, and finally that bill was withdrawn. A committee of five was appointed and Mr. Bennett made himself chairman of the committee. This committee brought in another bill. I am not going to discuss the bill because it is not for that purpose I bring up the question at the moment. I bring it up in order to say that because of the experience we had gone through in western Canada, hon. members on the other side of the house should be warned, particularly those in the C.C.F. group, that the kind of suggestions they have been making here this afternoon are not the suggestions that are going to settle the wheat question in western Canada.
6036	HOUSE OF
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus I am speaking from memory when I say this, and I may be a little out on my figures -if my friends look them up and find I am a little out, I hope they will not say I was attempting to misrepresent the facts here or say something I knew to be incorrect-my memory is that back in 1929, after we had a strong wheat pool in existence for a little better than four years, the initial payment on wheat had been built up to a fairly high level. Just as gentlemen across the floor of the house are saying now: "You should make this initial payment as high as you can, you should make it ten cents higher than the price is now"-according to one of the resolutions-"and start off from there", well, that is exactly the same kind of argument that was used with the wheat pools back in 1929. And when the wheat pool did that-and I am talking about the Saskatchewan wheat pool- when they thought that a dollar was high enough, they were compelled by the delegates to put it at $1.25.
Now, we went through that year. We had enormous losses, because the price of wheat went down. I say "we", because I was a member of it and I am still a member of it, and had something to do with starting it up in the first place. And so we took the losses that year because we set the initial payment too high, and because we were not permitted to lower it until sufficient wheat went on the market for the pools to have very considerable losses.
Now, the next year Mr. Bennett agreed to become more or less responsible for the losses they had incurred by guaranteeing the pools at the banks, guaranteeing their accounts, and allowing them to go on for a time on the condition that they allowed him to appoint a chairman, a one-man board, who would go ahead and handle wheat. Mr. McFarland was put in charge of wheat. And then, during the year that followed, the provinces were appealed to to put up money or rather to put up security against money that had been lost by the wheat pools. And the three provinces did that.
The outcome of that was that the Saskatchewan government, a province where more than half the wheat is grown, became responsible for something well over $20 million. The legislation was put through the house while I was a member of it; as a matter of fact, while I was leading the opposition. And I opposed some of it. Nevertheless the legislation went through. But it tied up the wheat pool in Saskatchewan over a twenty-year period. And, do you know, it is only three or four years ago that the pool was celebrating having made the last payment on that loss that was taken at that time.


Why was it taken? It was taken because the delegates who met at pool meetings in 1929 insisted upon a high initial payment, putting the pool into a position where they had to get the guarantee of governments in order to be able to carry on at all. And so the government stated how the policy was going to be conducted, and they put Mr. McFarland in charge of handling the wheat.
I do not know whether Mr. McFarland was told what to do. I only know that what he did do was to build up a greater and greater surplus during the time he was there. And when we came into office, or shortly after we came in, he had 298 million bushels of wheat in store, in 1935. Well, we asked him to sell it. My hon. friends the other night were calling this a fire sale. We asked him to sell the wheat. Why did we ask him to sell it? We asked him to sell it because we were of the opinion that to pile up wheat in this country and to hold it off the market with the idea you are going to improve the price was a wrong policy to follow; and that, as a matter of fact, the only way in which you could improve the price was to have the wheat eaten up at some price people were prepared to pay.
So we said, "Sell it". He said he would not sell it; so we got a new board. The new board sold the wheat with the result that in 1936 wheat averaged $1.22 a bushel, whereas it had been in the 80's at the time the order to sell was issued. And then the next year it was $1.31 a bushel. And so the farmer made the difference between about 84 or 86 cents a bushel as it was when the action was taken and $1.22 as the average in one year and $1.31 in the other.
All I am suggesting tonight is, that in so far as the farmers of western Canada are concerned-and that does not include very many fellows in the C.C.F. group-they are not going to have a board that is operating for them take the same kind of position again. They know what the results are. They know that a minister who comes here to this house and indicates that he has a clear line of policy for selling this wheat and getting it on the market is right. I made a statement the other day similar to what I am making now. I was speaking out in Saskatchewan; and of course when you are talking in the open air at a meeting, where they have loud speakers, covering about 40 acres, you cannot judge the attitude of listeners very well. But three or four men came to me after the speech was over and they said, "There was only one remark we heard while you were making that speech". I might say that they were not all speaking to me at the one time. Each one said, "The only remark we heard them making was this, 'He is dead right' ".

If my hon. friends are doing as the hon. member for Rosthern suggested they were doing-that is, if they are just trying to get votes-then I suggest they had better change their tune a little bit. Because after all the farmers in western Canada, particularly in Saskatchewan where more than half the wheat is grown, know this question just as well as any member in this house. They know what is in their interests, and they know what is not in their interests. And because they know I believe they are in support of what the government is doing at the present time.
My hon. friends in the C.C.F. have been very anxious during the last two or three days to say that the farmer in Saskatchewan is prosperous. It is not a month since they were panning me in every newspaper and on every platform in western Canada because I had said that the farmers were getting along better at the present time than they had at any other time in my experience. And now they come here and try to compete with one another in telling us that the farmer in Saskatchewan is well off.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Mang).

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
My hon. friends apparently are getting concerned about the hon. member for Qu'Appelle quoting their leader in the province of Saskatchewan, who happens to be the premier of Saskatchewan. Well, all the hon. member for Qu'Appelle did was to take the pamphlets that are being mailed through the mail every morning. I know that because I get one every morning. And the pamphlet quoted here the other night by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle was a pamphlet which I got a few days earlier telling me about the wonderful prosperity we have among farmers in Saskatchewan. As a matter of fact they said that while other provinces may be going down in the matter of returns and while other provinces may not be coming down in the matter of the cost of putting their products out, they went on to prove that Saskatchewan was in a better position than any of the other provinces.
Well, if they are I am very glad to hear it, because that is where I farm myself; and I know something about what farmers' returns are in Saskatchewan. I know something about what the condition of the farmer is today, as compared with the condition of the farmer in any other year since the beginning of the first war. And, knowing that, I am in agreement with some of the things which the Saskatchewan government said. But I am sure my hon. friends who represent the C.C.F. party in this house did not get very
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus much out of what he said to back up anything they have been saying lately. They have been suggesting that the farmer is going down and down. And when they are making that statement, knowing that probably there is not much to back it up, then they change it by saying, "If he is not going down and down, all right, he will be some day."
Well, we have been hearing that ever since the war ended. These gentlemen must pray every night that we will get a depression in Canada. When they get up to express themselves in this house and outside of it that is what they continuously say, and most people who do pray talk about the things they pray about. So these gentlemen over there no doubt hold forth on that ground. Is it the pamphlet published by the government of Saskatchewan which changed their tune?
Well, the farmer can stand more for his wheat. As a matter of fact, quite a lot of people thought he might get $2 or more for it. I recall one of them who was expressing these views very freely a while ago. A newspaperman came to me while I was out west there last week and asked me what I thought about it. I said: "Well, I have learned long ago not to be too free with prophecies with regard to the price of wheat".
That is only recently.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
He said: "You are just as bad to get a statement out of as my friend who was talking about it a short time ago and saying that we as farmers out here should not think of anything else but getting the high price which the governments were asking for their wheat at the time the international wheat agreement was under discussion". Well, I said to him at the time, and I am going to say it here, that fortunately or unfortunately, whichever it might be, depending on what you are thinking, we must depend on selling a greater part of the wheat, or at least more wheat to Britain than we sell to any other country in the world if we are going to market our wheat, and Britain no doubt will have something to say about what she pays for it.
We are not doing something any different from what we have always done in that regard. We do discuss these things with the British; we do discuss them with our United States friends to the south; and the only time, you know, that Canada did not discuss it with our United States friends to the south was back in 1932, and everybody knows that this government was not in power then. And what happened to wheat? When it was not discussed with the United States,

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus when they did not know what we were going to do and we did not know what they were going to do, then the price of wheat was, as the minister said the other day, as low as 46 cents a bushel. As a matter of fact, I remember selling wheat that year for 26 cents a bushel.
Because you did not discuss it with the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Partly, because you did not when you were in the government.
Because you did not discuss it with the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That question was not discussed with the United States.
That was not the reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: But, as the minister has been telling you from time to time-
That was not the reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
-we do keep in close touch with our United States friends to the south. We keep in touch with them with regard to the marketing of products in their country and with regard to feeding people in different parts of the world who require to be fed, and we try to co-operate in such a way as to get not only their farmers but our own farmers the best possible return for the products they are selling, and more particularly for their wheat.
Something has been said about the costs going up. I have been told during the last two or three weeks by people who sell the most expensive commodities that the farmer buys in western Canada that they are not making many sales out there at present. Now that is true. My friend says it is right. Of course it is right. But there is more than one reason why it is right. The chief reason is that during the war farmers could not buy new machinery at all. They were refused the right to buy, with the result that when the war was over the equipment on every farm in western Canada was run down to such a state that farmers had to get new equipment, and unfortunately perhaps for us we had to compete with the Korean war in getting it and the prices were high. But nevertheless the returns were sufficiently high that farmers could go and buy, in spite of that fact. As hon. members from Saskatchewan know, we have I think the most advanced implement legislation there is in any province in Canada out in Saskatchewan. It has been there for a long time.
I have no doubt that by the time this gets out in print the present government out there will be taking credit for it, but it happened away back in 1915, so that there is not much 

credit coming to them. It has been amended from time to time, and as the law now stands it is almost impossible for a man out in that province to get an implement unless he is able to pay about 50 per cent in cash. And that is not a bad thing for him either.
But he has been buying implements under that legislation and he has been getting himself equipped until today-I think every hon. member who comes from that section of the country will agree-he is as well equipped or a little better equipped than he ever was before, and equipped with expensive machinery. The only worry that some of us have had about it is whether he will get the machinery entirely paid for before he runs into difficulties in connection with the marketing of his wheat and the returns which he obtains for it when he does market it. If he is able to pay off anything that he owes on the machinery and go on operating from there he will be doing very well.
What the implement companies tell me is that during the last year, and more so during this year, their sales have been going down very materially. But they know that that is not only because there have been some reductions in the prices of commodities in 1953 as compared with 1951. They make their comparisons between 1953, and 1948 and 1949. They know that one of the reasons is that the farmers are equipped with good implements, and therefore at the present time they are not buying more. They are able to get along, and my hope is-I am sure it is the hope of every hon. member who comes from western Canada-that our farmers will go along with the kind of equipment which they require in order to do the job that they are doing efficiently, and that they will not be led into investing too much in farm implements and other equipment, particularly if they can get along well without getting that new equipment. The implement people think that that is what they are doing. They think the farmers still remember the days when they incurred considerable indebtedness in order to get the things that they required.
Hon. members on the other side of the house, and particularly the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough), said this afternoon: Yes, of course it is true that the indebtedness of the farmers has gone down. The mortgages are not as high as they were; they are paying them off and conditions are better today than they were at some other time, and what I am praying for-and I am sure my friends will pray along with me-is that we shall get along with the marketing of this wheat.
Why, we have had the three biggest crops that we have ever grown in western Canada.

Well, you can come here and quote statistics that the farmer has more wheat than he ever had before. The fact is that he grew so much wheat in the last three years-he grew more than he ever grew before-that he could not possibly have been in any other position than to have more wheat than he ever had before. I am still agreeing with the Minister of Trade and Commerce that it is not a bad thing for the farmers in western Canada after those three years experience to have some wheat on their farms and to be in the position that they are today where they can sell a whole year's wheat over the year that is ahead or over the months that are ahead, even if they have a poor crop. When they do, if they do get the return which is offered now, and if they do not get any more than that, the fact that they have produced on an average about twice as much, from 75 per cent to 100 per cent more than they did before in other three-year periods, they will have more in cash for the labour that they put forth in order to produce that wheat than they have ever had on any other occasion.
After all the labour he puts forth and the costs he puts into his implements and other requirements are the real costs of producing so much wheat. If he gets 50 per cent more than he expected to get or 75 per cent more than he expected to get, then it is not a case of his costs having gone up as compared with what he sells, it is a case of his sales going up as compared with what he had to pay in costs. And those farmers tell me that so long as we have a Minister of Trade and Commerce who is optimistic, who does think that he can sell the wheat-because he thinks he can sell it, he probably will-then they are in the best position that they can possibly be in.
Even my hon. friend who runs a hardware store in Moose Jaw will agree that if his business is run on that principle he will be all right for quite a long time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am in a very difficult position because, like myself, hon. members have seen the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) rise on three previous occasions, and perhaps at this time one of them might yield because I think that would be the best thing to do. I appreciate the cooperation of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe).

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Ross Thatcher (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
speechtext:
I will take only about five minutes, Mr. Speaker. I think there is one fact which has emerged in this debate so far. Whether hon. members come from the east or the west, whether they are Liberal, Conservative, C.C.F. or Social Credit, after listening to this 83276-382
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus debate I think they must realize that the western farmer today is having marketing difficulties.
We are in real trouble with our wheat. This is not a matter of levity in western Canada. Our granaries are jammed to capacity, our elevators are filled, and we have wheat lying out in the fields. It appears moreover, that we will have another bumper crop this year.
In view of these facts our farmers naturally are concerned. Thus it seems to me that the main purpose of this debate today should be to discuss what can be done about our huge wheat surplus; what can be done about this 700 million bushels of wheat which is presently on hand.
I listened to the spokesman of the Conservative party today. I heard their amendment to the effect that this house regrets the government has failed to deal effectively with the problem. I am inclined to agree with them, but what alternative have the Conservatives to offer? I listened to government spokesmen also, including the minister tonight, and I did not hear them propose any solution over and above what they have given us so far.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have two or three concrete suggestions I would like to place before the house if I can do it within the five minutes at my disposal. I do not think there is any easy or obvious solution to our wheat surplus. I do not feel there is any magic formula. I am convinced there is no simple answer. But I do believe there are a few steps which could be taken. I feel that no one in parliament should treat this wheat problem with indifference, and I do not thinir we should meet the problem with inaction. On the other hand, I do not think hon. members should panic.
Speaking personally I cannot get too worried about having had bumper crops in western Canada. I cannot get too worried about having too much wheat. It is a lovely problem to have. But despite the fact that we should not treat our surplus as a liability, there are some steps we have to consider taking without delay. I agree with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that following the United States procedure of cutting acreage is not the answer, and I do not think a price war is any satisfactory solution.
What can we do? First of all I think the Department of Agriculture should go out to our farmers in western Canada and urge them to feed as much grain as possible to livestock, hogs, turkeys, chickens, and sheep. I have always believed that in western Canada it would be a sensible thing to have a

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus more diversified agricultural economy. It is good insurance in case we hit low prices for grain, and it is good insurance in case we hit a drought.
Today with so much grain on hand, surely it is more sensible than ever for every single farmer in the west to get into diversified farming. I know some hon. members will probably say, "Well, if they go into cattle and hogs we will then have a surplus of meat." To a degree that may be quite correct. But, Mr. Speaker, I do not think our farmers today are taking full advantage of the Geneva agreement provisions, which permit us to sell these products to the United States.
For example, where cattle are concerned, there is today a cent and a half per pound tariff on the first 200,000 calves and the first 400,000 cattle of 700 pounds or more which we sell annually. Last year we sold to the United States only 2,000 calves and 45,000 head of cattle.
As far as hogs are concerned, under the Geneva agreement we are entitled to sell all the hogs that we can produce if we want to pay a tariff of one cent per pound. Yet last year we only sent 20,232 swine to the United States. As far as sheep and lambs are concerned, we can send unlimited quantities down there at a tariff of $3 per head. But last year we sent only 153 sheep to our southern neighbour.
As far as poultry is concerned there is a tariff of two cents per pound and there is no quota. But last year we sent only 227 turkeys and 45,000 poultry of other kinds. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say again that if we can be sure that the United States will not renege on their commitments under the Geneva agreement, I think there is a very real market for our farmers in which to sell livestock and poultry in the United States. I suggest this is the first practical method which we should follow to get rid of our huge grain surplus. Let the government help the farmers to help themselves. I think that literally dozens of millions of bushels of wheat could be marketed in such a manner.
In the second place, Mr. Speaker, I am not convinced that the government is doing a good selling job as far as the iron curtain countries are concerned. The other day I mentioned that I did not think the Department of Trade and Commerce has done such a good job of selling. Only a month ago the Russian ambassador said that his country was willing to buy wheat. Two officials from the Russian embassy called at the Department of Trade and Commerce, but all our officials did was to give them a few prices. They


did not follow up the sale in any way at all.
I do not think aggressiveness was shown nor selling capacity. I do not feel that advantage is being taken of that potential market.
We know that Russia, China, and other countries behind the iron curtain are very badly in need of foodstuffs. When we have 700 million bushels of wheat in western Canada I simply cannot see why we cannot get together. I think something should be done by the government to increase sales to eastern nations.
In the third place, and I am rushing, I think our government should do a little more than it is doing as far as our immigration program is concerned. I think it is sensible for our government to bring people into Canada to consume our grain and foodstuffs. I fully realize that there is considerable agitation throughout the country at the present time for curtailing immigration. The trade unions are a little bit afraid of it. But as far as our farmers are concerned, Mr. Speaker, I think there is nothing more realistic than to have a larger domestic market right here at home. I hope the government will not yield to some of the pressure which has been put upon them recently to reduce the immigration quota. I think we are always likely to have a farm marketing problem as long as our population remains as low as 15 million.
I shall close in a minute but before I do so I want to say that I think the Minister of of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) should be interested in barter deals.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Huh!

The minister says "huh" but there may be some countries interested in buying our wheat which would like to indulge in barter. I admit it is not ordinarily a good way to do business, but if it is the only way in which we can sell wheat to Russia or some other country, then let us have barter. Even in my own business I sometimes have customers who cannot pay cash immediately and if that is the case I extend long term credit. Might I then suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that perhaps some potential purchasers of wheat need long term credit, and if that is so let us extend it to them. I believe too, Mr. Speaker, that it might be sensible for Canada to consider giving very modest gifts of wheat to some of the needy nations of the world. I certainly would not recommend going overboard-there are sensible limits to such a program. However, such a program should be considered.
Mr. Speaker, I have tried to stay within my five minutes. Before sitting down, may I repeat that there are several things this government could do. If they do not act the

western farmer is going to be in trouble; and as soon as the western farmer is in trouble, the difficulty will be like a snowball, it will react right through our economy as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock?

speechtext:
Probably we did not have the money then; but Mr. Speaker, that is not the issue. If it had not been for the sharp interjection or interruption, Mr. Speaker, you would probably have called me to order for even answering something that is so irrelevant to the issue that is before us.
The Minister of Agriculture speaks about the way in which we sold wheat. Every hon. member within sound of my voice knows that every elevator in Canada was bulging and overloaded with unsold wheat when the Conservative party came into power in 1930, and that every lumber yard that had not been burned for insurance was overloaded with lumber that had not been sold. Nobody knows that better than does the Minister of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I did not burn any.

There was not a sale for anything in Canada when his party went out of power and one of the reasons was that which the minister has mentioned tonight. From 1921 to 1930 their eyes were cast north and south again. In 1921 we sold to the United Kingdom more beef, more bacon and more wheat than we have sold in practically any other year until this late war came on. Whenever we mention an imperial conference they scoff at the suggestion. They think we are thinking of nothing but the old empire, the British commonwealth and the union jack.
On the hustings the Minister of Agriculture and his cohorts will say that this party talk about trade but keep themselves wrapped up in the union jack. But down through the years, for the last 50 years-yes, for the last 75 years-we have had a favourable trade balance with the United Kingdom. As the Minister of Agriculture has so well said tonight-and no one knows it better than he-the best market in the world available to the Canadian people for wheat and for mixed farming products is the United Kingdom market. The only other market that is better than that one for agricultural products is the market right here at home; and that


market is not improved by listening to Washington. To say that the price of wheat in Canada went down as low as it did in 1930 because we did not discuss it with Washington when the United States of America were selling their wheat in Buffalo at exactly the same price is just nonsense. Why, Mr. Speaker, such nonsense in this issue is not even politically attractive. It is only a political nuisance.
It surely is.

I hear "carried" outside the curtains, the echoes made by those who keep speaking inside the curtains. I know that remarks like that are more popular out there than they are in here. But if you look at the spectacle of what has happened, here is what we find. The Minister of Agriculture will remember it very well. I cannot recall the exact statistics because I did not intend to speak and I have not any notes. However, I will do as the Minister of Agriculture has done so well in the past and say this: If my statement is not exactly correct, it is not an error of intention. In fact, I have heard him modify his remarks in that way on many occasions previously. It is a neat way of being reckless and yet having people believe that you are honest.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Go ahead. Be reckless.

No, I am not as reckless as the hon. member even though he does not speak as much in the house as some others. I am not even reckless in my thinking. I suggested a few years ago that we should sell our wheat more or less according to the law of supply and demand and that we should not try to be so generous as to accept less than the world would give us for our wheat. In those years the farmers of western Canada, those intelligent friends of the minister, were losing $300 million to $400 million a year by having to take much less than the world price. I can well recall that at that time the minister said to me: You have not as much confidence in the British traders as I have. I remember saying to him that very shortly he would find that the British traders would buy wheat where they could buy it the cheapest. I wonder whether he does not recall that. He nods his head in approval. Thanks for the sporting gesture of indicating that I was right once.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Oh no, I just recall it.

But now he suggests that we must sell where we can sell. I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and others have said the same thing at election time, that

this Howe-Gardiner salesmanship corporation has brought about the greatest fiasco of a gamble with somebody else's money that has ever been seen in any corporation in Canada. The Minister of Agriculture has got more butter than he knows what to do with. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is selling pork to Russia for one-quarter of what it cost. They have more wheat now that they cannot sell than has ever been stored in Canada with the exception of 1929 before the Liberals went out of power. The two high record years have been while they were in power. They were in power from 1921 to 1930, and remember, Mr. Speaker, that during those years we practically lost our whole British market. Here in this house in 1926 and 1927 they said that the great hope for the farmers of Canada was to sell their farm products to the United States. We have never believed that.
We do not believe that we can hope for a permanent agricultural market in those southern areas, in that great climate, in that rich agricultural country that produces surpluses of wheat and surpluses of almost everything else. We sold 255 million pounds of bacon to Britain in 1921. We sold $80 million worth of beef at a much lower price than the price of beef today. We sold all sorts of butter, eggs and bacon products, but by 1930 we were importing Danish bacon to feed our own people. It was being sold right in the minister's own province of Saskatchewan. They were taking your barley from Saskatchewan to fatten their hogs in Denmark and selling the bacon back to you so you free traders could eat Danish bacon in western Canada.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, they tell you what they have done to establish these markets. Now we have the spectacle again. We have more unsold wheat than anyone ever anticipated since confederation, and these are the gentlemen who now tell you about the sales that were made back in the thirties. We now have the spectacle of a group of men who refuse to negotiate with Britain, so much so that Britain refused to remain in the international wheat agreement deal and proceeded to buy wheat where she likes. Instead of getting a price of $2.05 they are now intimating tonight that we may even have to take $1.42.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Who intimated that?

I do not think it is a fair statement to suggest that the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that. I think he said it facetiously when somebody said we might have to take $1.42. He said we might have
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus to take another 10 cent drop, and I should not say that he suggested $1.42 because neither he nor anyone else would hope that we will have to take that. But it shows the trend of the times. It shows the change of policy. It shows the change of attitude that these gentlemen who refused $2.50 are now suggesting, even facetiously, that they will take the price that anyone else will give them. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said the other night that we will sell wheat where people will buy it. That is about the most sensible thing I have heard him say in the house in a long time-
Hear, hear.

-because the old law of supply and demand must control. I hear some hon. member saying "hear, hear". Of course, Mr. Speaker, you can get "hear, hear" from that side of the house on any kind of issue. If I suggested the highest kind of protection policy I bet that the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Schneider) would say "hear, hear". If I made the wildest free trade suggestion that has ever been proposed in the house I bet the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) would say "hear, hear". If I suggested a socialist program that would put my friends to the left to shame I bet there are three or four hon. gentlemen over here who would say "hear, hear" if they thought their leaders were not watching them. So, Mr. Speaker, it is a great party.
Hear, hear.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, that is the only thing they are in agreement about, when you suggest they are a great party, because they involve every stripe, every brand, every political temperament, every fickle idea in politics that there is in Canada and out on the hustings. Nobody knows what they all stand for; God only knows what they each stand for.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Hear, hear.

The result is that today we have no sound marketing policy. The Minister of Agriculture did not tell us what the policy is. The Minister of Trade and Commerce came here and said that we will sell as cheaply as anybody else in the world. We have no fiscal policy. God alone knows what the fiscal policy of the Liberal party is today. We have all sorts of textile products coming in here from other countries, heavy machinery, and men unemployed. Some of them on that side of the house want free trade, others want protection and the leaders are afraid to say. The right hon. gentleman

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus who is always glib would be afraid to rise tonight and say that he believes in free trade so far as these industries are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: You might be surprised.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce would not rise tonight and say: We will sell wheat as cheaply as anybody else and we will buy for the western farmers textiles and heavy machinery wherever we can buy the cheapest. It would not be fair to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) now because he is going to be judge over all pretty soon. But I know that in his heart of hearts he knows that he has been associated with the greatest conglomeration of mixed policies that the party has had since confederation. They have been all things to all industries; all things to all men, and all types of protection for all phases of policy. The only one who can laugh through it all is the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) because he has been on both sides so often.
The Minister of Agriculture prompted me to rise tonight when he suggested that I was among those responsible for the fiasco between 1930 and 1935.
Hear, hear.

Yes, they all say "hear, hear". Some of you younger members who are saying "hear, hear" were not even here. But, Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Finance so well said the other night, because he has moments of sincerity, no particular party was responsible for the fiasco of 1930.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Who said that?
He should explain that to these young hecklers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You must have been dreaming.

And they know it as well or they would not be worthy of being here. They know that there were 35 million people unemployed throughout the world, that there were 15 million people unemployed in the United States and two and a half million unemployed before this party came into power. Every elevator was filled with unsold wheat and every lumberyard was filled with unsold lumber. Every elevator today is filled with unsold wheat. If it had not been for pre-war, wartime and post-war policies that bailed the government out of a situation for which they had no policy this country would have noticed their weakness in fiscal policy long ago.
I am not going to delay the house. I do not believe in holding the house after ten o'clock.


The group that sits to your right, Mr. Speaker, no doubt like to rush things through when the session is drawing to a close. In fact, in the quarter of a century that I have been here I have noticed there is a cunning device used to try to get contentious measures through, either late on Friday night or some time after ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: You were never here late on Friday night.

I am glad my hon. friend misses me because if he were not here the fact probably would not be noticed at all. I do feel that this is not a rule we should follow. I would have preferred an adjournment tonight and continue the debate tomorrow. I wish to say that the wheat problem in this country is a serious one. I know that everyone hopes we can sell all the unsold wheat possible.
I am not one of those to whom the Minister of Agriculture referred who is hoping for a depression in this country. We have a serious situation. Personally, I do not believe the government has handled it well. I believe they thought that No. 1 hard wheat could be sold for whatever they wished to ask for it. They refused to take a reasonable price. Fortunately, they have now changed their minds and are ready to deal on a sensible basis. Whether or not wheat prices go lower, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, the thing is, and I say this as a farmer myself-
Oh, oh.

My hon. friend laughs, but J have always lived on a farm and have been responsible for growing quite a lot of wheat. While we do not grow as much as some of my friends in western Canada, and the Minister of Agriculture gibes me a bit, I think perhaps I have farmed more than he has. In the last two years his government has been chiefly farming the farmers, so far as selling their products is concerned.
I say that there is no farmer within the sound of my voice who wants to be pap fed by the state by means of subsidies. I believe we have to get down to a common sense business basis. On this point I do find myself somewhat in agreement with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, even though it is a new idea of his, that we must sell where we can sell. If the price is not as good as we had expected, it is an honest price. As a farmer, I do not expect other people to pay for my lower prices on wheat.
I realize hon. members are anxious to conclude the debate, but since I understand there are some other speakers I should like to move the adjournment of the debate at this stage.
No.

There have been two very provocative 40-minute speeches delivered from the other side since eight o'clock, and I think hon. members should not be asked to allow those provocative speeches to go unanswered at this time of night.
Business of the House
On motion of Mr. Nicholson the debate was adjourned.
